#378. Havells unveils battery energy storage systems

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (658 w)
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Pv-magazine

Havells unveils battery energy storage systems

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (658 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Pv-magazine

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Havells India showcased its battery energy storage systems (BESS) at the REI Expo 2026, highlighting its energy storage solutions as part of its broader renewable energy portfolio, which also includes hybrid inverters, EV chargers, solar inverters and modules.
  • The company established a dedicated renewables business unit in April to expand its presence across the sector.
  • According to recent reports, “Our primary focus is to address the residential and commercial and industrial (C&I) segments first,” said Reshu Madan, President & SBU Head, Havells.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Havells India showcased its battery energy storage systems (BESS) at the REI Expo 2026, highlighting its energy storage solutions as part of its broader renewable energy portfolio, which also includes hybrid inverters, EV chargers, solar inverters and modules.

The company established a dedicated renewables business unit in April to expand its presence across the sector.

According to recent reports, “Our primary focus is to address the residential and commercial and industrial (C&I) segments first,” said Reshu Madan, President & SBU Head, Havells. “We also proposal to expand into utility-scale and agricultural applications.”.

Havells has partnered with Norway-based Pixii to introduce modular battery storage solutions with software-defined controls in India. Its initial portfolio will cover applications from 3 kW to 125 kW, with intends to expand into larger systems. The company also plans to offer integrated solar-plus-storage solutions for residential, commercial and institutional customers.

Havells’ modular battery storage system portfolio will include the PowerShaper family, featuring the PowerShaper XLP with capacities of 112kW/225kW, and the PowerNode family, starting at 125 kW for larger commercial and industrial applications.

“The modular design will allow individual units to be added or replaced while the system is operating, enabling customers to configure storage capacity according to their requirements,” said Aseem Goyal, BU Head – Renewables, Havells India Ltd. “Neither undersizing nor oversizing will be required. That’s where a lot of innovation plays a role,” Goyal added.

The partnership with Pixii is intended to bring the technology to Indian customers at competitive costs while leveraging Havells’ distribution network and installer base. Havells also prepares to introduce a new product family, MegaNode, for utility-scale energy storage applications in the future.The company sees opportunities for off-grid and microgrid storage in remote areas, despite the expansion of grid connectivity.

“Off-grid markets are gradually going away. The Indian government has done a fantastic job in ensuring that electricity reaches every corner of the country,” said Goyal. “However, pockets in states such as Uttar Pradesh and Bihar, along with remote locations, continue to offer opportunities for off-grid and microgrid installations.”.

Mining operations are another potential market for battery storage, Goyal added.

Havells’ solar module portfolio includes monocrystalline PERC bifacial and TOPCon technologies, with TOPCon modules rated up to 620 Wp. The manufacturer manufactures some grid-tied inverter models in India, while importing higher-capacity models.

Havells is also a strategic investor in Goldi Solar, which has 16 GW of solar module manufacturing capacity and is expanding into solar cell production.

The partnership combines Goldi Solar’s manufacturing capabilities with Havells’ distribution network and customer reach. “Goldi plays more on the IPP market side, and we play on our strengths on the distribution market side,” said Goyal.

In a recent development, havells manufactures and markets non-DCR modules under its own brand. The company expects to secure ALMM List-II approval for its DCR modules soon.

The company is also localising its battery storage supply chain, focusing on four key components: power electronics, batteries, software and racking systems. It has already started localising its energy management software and is working on localising the racking system. It plans to begin local battery manufacturing in the near future.

Havells aims to strengthen its position in the renewable energy market by moving beyond individual product offerings towards integrated solutions.

Recent findings suggest that “Our aim is to gain the confidence of customers and deliver a better consumer experience. This will not come only from the product; it will come from providing a complete solution,” stated Reshu Madan, President & SBU Head at Havells. The company expects to become a significant player in the renewable energy sector over the next three to four years.

Product reliability, warranties and after-sales support are also central to its strategy. Havells offers a 10-year warranty on its inverters, compared to industry offerings that typically range from six to eight years, according to the company. Its battery storage products come with a minimum 10-year warranty, extendable by another five years.

#377. Fresnel-based agrivoltaic system redistributes sunlight beneath solar modules to boost crop yields

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (576 w)
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Pv-magazine

Fresnel-based agrivoltaic system redistributes sunlight beneath solar modules to boost crop yields

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (576 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Pv-magazine

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A research team in India has proposed a novel agrivoltaic system that uses linear-diverging Fresnel optics to redistribute transmitted sunlight into shaded regions.
  • It has been revealed that fresnel optics use thin, lightweight lenses or sheets with precisely engineered grooves to bend and redirect incoming light.
  • It has been revealed that “The central novelty of our research is demonstrating that how sunlight is distributed beneath photovoltaic modules is as key as how much sunlight crops receive over the course of a day,” noted corresponding author Adersh Asok to pv magazine.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A research team in India has proposed a novel agrivoltaic system that uses linear-diverging Fresnel optics to redistribute transmitted sunlight into shaded regions. Named Even Solar Sharing Agrivoltaics (ESS-AV), it uses diverging Fresnel optics, which are thin, transparent sheets patterned with tiny grooves that spread incoming sunlight outward.

It has been revealed that fresnel optics use thin, lightweight lenses or sheets with precisely engineered grooves to bend and redirect incoming light. Unlike conventional lenses, they can control how sunlight is concentrated or dispersed while requiring significantly less material.

It has been revealed that “The central novelty of our research is demonstrating that how sunlight is distributed beneath photovoltaic modules is as key as how much sunlight crops receive over the course of a day,” noted corresponding author Adersh Asok to pv magazine. “Our ESS-AV system continuously redistributes sunlight into shaded regions, producing a more homogeneous light environment beneath the photovoltaic array.”.

Asok explained that the conventional fixed-tilt agrivoltaic configurations often create alternating regions of intense sunlight and deep shade, which might influence crop growth underneath. “Importantly, we compared ESS-AV with a conventional checkerboard agrivoltaic configuration having identical PV coverage and nominal electrical capacity. This enabled us to isolate the influence of instantaneous light distribution on crop productivity without compromising electricity generation,” he added.

The researchers compared two 1.1 kW rooftop agrivoltaic systems at Thiruvananthapuram, southern India, each with 15 PV modules and 50% PV coverage. One used a conventional checkerboard layout, while the ESS-AV system incorporated Fresnel sheets between modules to redistribute sunlight. The team designed the optics in AutoCAD, simulated them in COMSOL Multiphysics, and fabricated them using a laser machine.

The team grew spearmint hydroponically for 60 days beneath both systems and in an uncovered rooftop control. The team measured crop-level light intensity and uniformity, temperature, and humidity, then assessed plant dimensions, fresh biomass, photosynthetic pigments, water status, membrane damage, and phenolic and flavonoid content. Essential-oil composition was analyzed using gas chromatography mass spectrometry, and treatment differences were evaluated statistically.

“The most striking finding was that our ESS-AV system produced approximately 13% more spearmint fresh biomass than the conventional checkerboard configuration, even though both systems provided comparable daily average photosynthetic light and electricity generation,” Asok stated. “In fact, the measured average photosynthetic photon flux density (PPFD) was slightly lower under ESS-AV than under the checkerboard system. However, ESS-AV achieved instantaneous light uniformity above 0.922, compared with approximately 0.21 for the conventional configuration.”.

The ESS-AV system also achieved a land equivalent ratio (LER) of 1.81 relative to full rooftop PV coverage and 2.04 relative to conventional ground-mounted PV installations, indicating improved combined agricultural and electricity productivity per unit area. “By eliminating separate maintenance gaps between PV rows, our analysis suggests that relative PV installation capacity could potentially increase from approximately 50% to 73% of a conventional ground-mounted PV reference, while preserving the intended optical design,” added the researcher.

“Our long-term objective is to move beyond treating agricultural productivity and solar electricity generation as competing objectives,” Asok concluded. “Instead, we aim to develop agrivoltaic infrastructure in which the optical environment can be engineered to support crop productivity while maintaining commercially relevant electricity generation.”.

The research “Beyond daily average irradiance: Instantaneous homogeneous light distribution unlocks higher productivity in fixed-tilt agrivoltaics” was presented in Renewable Energy. Scientists from India’s CSIR–National Institute for Interdisciplinary Science and Technology and the Academy of Scientific and Innovative Research (AcSIR) have contributed to the research.

Vietnamese provinces back floating PV projects

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (496 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Pv-magazine

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Authorities in three Vietnamese provinces have advanced prepares for utility-scale floating solar projects, with installations ranging from 30 MW to over 300 MW.
  • The province of Gai Lai in southcentral Vietnam is preparing a groundbreaking ceremony for a 35 MW floating solar project this week.
  • The Bau Can floating solar power plant is expected to span 47 hectares in total, 30 of which will cover the surface on the Bau Can lake.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Authorities in three Vietnamese provinces have advanced prepares for utility-scale floating solar projects, with installations ranging from 30 MW to over 300 MW.

The province of Gai Lai in southcentral Vietnam is preparing a groundbreaking ceremony for a 35 MW floating solar project this week.

The Bau Can floating solar power plant is expected to span 47 hectares in total, 30 of which will cover the surface on the Bau Can lake.

Local press lists Bau Can Solar Energy joint stock manufacturer (JSC) as the investor, with total costs expected to reach VND 613 billion ($23.8 million).

It has been revealed that installation is due for completion in July 2028, with commissioning scheduled for a month later. Once completed, the project is expected to supply nearly 59 GWh annually over a 50 year operating life.

The province of Lam Dong, southern Vietnam, has backed investment in a planned floating solar array to be installed on the Dak Sin 1 hydroelectric reservoir in Quang Ting commune.

The floating PV project has a planned capacity of 30 MW. It will utilise around 33 hectares of land, 31 of which will be on the water surface.

In a recent development, it will be implemented by VRG Dak Nong JSC, with total investment expected to reach VND 499.5 billion. The project is due to be completed and put into operation by the fourth quarter of 2028.

The province of Dak Lak, just south of Gai Lai province, recently granted a 50-year lease for a large-scale floating solar project to be built on the Srepok 3 hydropower reservoir, located across Ea Nuol and Ea Wer communes.

Developer Srepok 3 Solar Power JSC has been given permission to cover 354 hectares of the reservoir with the solar installation.

A letter confirming the approval states the developer has full exemption from land rental payments for the entire 50 year lease period but says it must complete the relevant legal procedures before using the reservoir’s water surface.

The letter does not state a planned capacity for the floating PV project but details on the provincial government of Dak Lak’s website states a proposed capacity of 304 MW, alongside investment of VND 7.661 trillion. It also gives a target commissioning date by the end of 2027.

Sources indicate that earlier this month, authorities in Dak Lak approved a 452 MW floating solar project on the Ea Sup Thuong reservoir. The project is scheduled for completion by the end of 2028 and would rank among the world’s largest inland floating PV installations.

In a recent development, the country’s Ministry of Industry and Trade recently announced new regional electricity generation price ceilings for ground-mounted and floating solar projects. Floating solar projects are subject to higher ceilings than ground-mounting projects, ranging from VND 1,340.21 ($0.052)/kWh in the south to VND 1,939.74/kWh in the north.

Vietnam’s solar capacity surpassed 19 GW by the end of 2025, with around 586 MW of solar added last year.

#375. Satellite imagery reveals vegetation recovery at solar plant in semi-arid region of China

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (845 w)
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Pv-magazine

Satellite imagery reveals vegetation recovery at solar plant in semi-arid region of China

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (845 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Pv-magazine

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers at China’s Hohai University have examined seasonal vegetation changes at the 21 GW Gonghe Talatan solar power cluster in Gonghe County, Hainan Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture, Qinghai province, China, and have found that vegetation levels surpassed pre-construction levels within two years of PV installation.
  • In a recent development, the region is characterized by predominantly flat terrain at an average elevation of approximately 2,920 meters and a cold, arid to semi-arid climate.
  • Industry observers note that the scientists used a multiscale analytical approach combining high-resolution satellite imagery with long-term satellite observations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers at China’s Hohai University have examined seasonal vegetation changes at the 21 GW Gonghe Talatan solar power cluster in Gonghe County, Hainan Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture, Qinghai province, China, and have found that vegetation levels surpassed pre-construction levels within two years of PV installation.

In a recent development, the region is characterized by predominantly flat terrain at an average elevation of approximately 2,920 meters and a cold, arid to semi-arid climate. Average annual temperatures stand at 4.1 C, while annual precipitation reaches 303 mm, nearly 88% of which falls between May and September. Annual evaporation amounts to approximately 1,800 mm, while the region receives more than 2,900 hours of sunshine per year and experiences significant wind-driven sand movement.

Industry observers note that the scientists used a multiscale analytical approach combining high-resolution satellite imagery with long-term satellite observations. They analyzed four Beijing-3 satellite images acquired between May and August 2025, each with a spatial resolution of 1.2 meters. The images enabled them to identify solar panels and assess vegetation growing between them using the normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI), calculated from red and near-infrared reflectance.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers manually mapped the solar panels to exclude panel-covered areas from the vegetation analysis. They also used Landsat satellite imagery with a spatial resolution of 30 meters to track vegetation changes between 2008 and 2025. The datasets were processed through Google Earth Engine to generate annual maximum NDVI measurements.

Industry observers note that to assess vegetation differences, the team compared conditions within the solar plants with those in adjacent control areas extending up to 120 meters beyond the plant boundaries. Areas overlapping with neighboring PV installations were excluded, while only control areas larger than 500 square meters were retained to ensure reliable comparisons.

It has been revealed that the researchers also examined monthly vegetation changes from May to August using Landsat imagery covering 2024 to 2026. To minimize interference from solar panels in the lower-resolution Landsat images, they developed a filtering method based on panel coverage. They tested five coverage thresholds ranging from 30% to 70% to assess their influence on NDVI measurements.

Sources indicate that for the long-term analysis, they retained pixels with solar panel coverage of 50% or less. Vegetation records were then aligned according to each plant’s construction year, enabling the researchers to examine changes from five years before installation to 10 years afterward. Plants installed in 2021, 2024, and 2025 were excluded from this analysis because of insufficient pre- and post-construction observations.

The analysis of 158 PV plant sites in 2025 indicated that vegetation within the installations was consistently greener than in surrounding areas, with average NDVI values within the plants being 11.5% higher than in adjacent control areas, with the largest difference recorded in August.

It has been revealed that landsat observations from 2024 to 2026 confirmed this pattern across all 12 monthly comparisons, with NDVI differences ranging from 3.5% to 10.7%. Long-term satellite data also revealed sustained improvements in vegetation conditions following PV construction.

The researchers found that NDVI exceeded pre-construction levels by 19.9% in the second year after installation and was, on average, 28.4% higher between the second and fifth years. Plants completed between 2013 and 2018 recorded increases ranging from 14.1% to 35.9%, with older installations generally showing stronger vegetation recovery.

“Generally, the NDVI within the PV plant polygons was slightly higher than that in the surrounding external areas,” the researchers explained. “This difference was particularly observed in the southern PV plant polygons, where vegetation greenness was obviously higher than that observed in the other PV plant polygons.”.

The researchers suggested that panel shading, reduced evaporation, lower wind speeds and rainfall redistribution could contribute to improved growing conditions. Water from panel cleaning and vegetation reseeding may also play a role, although these mechanisms were not directly verified.

They cautioned that climatic variability, uncertainties associated with satellite measurements and the lack of field observations limit the findings, which may not be directly applicable to regions with different environmental conditions.

Their findings are presented in the study “Impacts of large-scale centralized photovoltaic plant construction on vegetation: Satellite evidence from Gonghe photovoltaic park, China,” published in Information Geography.

Sources indicate that previous research has also highlighted the potential environmental benefits of large-scale PV installations in arid regions. In October 2024, scientists at China’s Xi’an University of Technology examined the ecological effects of a 1 GW solar installation at the Qinghai Gonghe Photovoltaic Park. They found that the installation achieved a higher environmental assessment score than surrounding areas, suggesting improvements in local microclimate conditions, soil properties, and plant and microbial diversity.

Sources indicate that more recently, researchers at the Chinese Academy of Sciences examined the cooling effects of eight solar plants in China’s arid regions. They found that PV installations can create localized cooling effects extending between 120 meters and 540 meters beyond their boundaries, with cooling intensity reaching 3.1 C in some locations. Vegetation responses varied depending on seasonal conditions, geographical location and plant design, suggesting that the ecological benefits of large-scale solar development are strongly site-dependent.

#374. Dutch researchers develop LEGO-like solar blocks combining luminescent concentrators and perovskite PV cells

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (829 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Pv-magazine

Dutch researchers develop LEGO-like solar blocks combining luminescent concentrators and perovskite PV cells

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (829 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Pv-magazine

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that researchers at Eindhoven University of Technology (TU/e) are developing colourful, LEGO-like building blocks capable of harvesting sunlight and converting it into electricity.
  • Industry observers note that the blocks are made from transparent polymers containing fluorescent dyes that absorb incoming light and re-emit it at longer wavelengths, according to lead researcher Martijn van Best.
  • “At one side of the block, we will attach customized photovoltaic cells, initially perovskite devices, to convert the emission light into electrical current,” Van Best said.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that researchers at Eindhoven University of Technology (TU/e) are developing colourful, LEGO-like building blocks capable of harvesting sunlight and converting it into electricity. The technology uses luminescent solar concentrators (LSCs) combined with photovoltaic cells, potentially opening up new opportunities for solar-powered educational toys, urban infrastructure and building-integrated photovoltaics (BIPV).

Industry observers note that the blocks are made from transparent polymers containing fluorescent dyes that absorb incoming light and re-emit it at longer wavelengths, according to lead researcher Martijn van Best. “The dyes absorb specific wavelengths of incident light, whether sunlight or interior, artificial lighting, and re-emit this light at a longer wavelength,” he told pv magazine. The light is then guided towards the edges of the blocks through total internal reflection, where photovoltaic cells can convert it into electricity.

“At one side of the block, we will attach customized photovoltaic cells, initially perovskite devices, to convert the emission light into electrical current,” Van Best said. He noted that the technology can operate under a range of lighting conditions, including indoors. “A distinct advantage of the luminescent solar concentrators (LSCs) is that they function well in both direct and indirect sunlight.”.

In a recent development, van Best also noted that the colour of the blocks will influence their performance. “They are also tough and colorful, although the color will affect electrical performance: red blocks will be more efficient than blue, for example,” he remarked.

The researchers expect the devices to achieve electrical conversion efficiencies below 10%, significantly lower than those of conventional crystalline silicon solar cells. Nevertheless, Van Best stressed that efficiency should not be the primary criterion for evaluating the technology, as the blocks are designed to combine electricity generation with other functions.

“Solar cells will always be more efficient than an LSC device, but the LSC has a different purpose, and is not only for generating electricity,” he said.

He pointed to previous applications of LSC technology in solar noise barriers, where sound insulation, appearance and transparency were more important than electricity generation. Similar principles could apply to bus shelters, urban furniture and building materials, allowing otherwise passive structures to generate power.

“So, efficiencies are expected to be modest but enough to power small objects locally such as LEDs or little motors in the case of the toy blocks, a bus shelter message board or advertising sign, without having to hide an unattractive solar panel or fear of it being stolen,” Van Best explained.

It has been revealed that the project remains at an early development stage. Initial research conducted by two master’s students has resulted in yellow and red blocks made from polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS), a transparent silicone polymer. The team has also developed optical simulations to predict their performance.

The researchers are now investigating how stacking multiple blocks affects light transmission and electricity generation. Another challenge involves integrating photovoltaic cells and electrical connections into an interlocking structure without compromising optical performance.

Recent findings suggest that van Best said Canadian project partner Block&Code has already addressed several electrical interconnection challenges, although further development is required to accommodate solar cells and optimise light guidance. The team must also establish dedicated measurement methods for three-dimensional LSC structures, an area that has received limited previous research attention.

Industry observers note that the first practical applications are expected to involve educational products rather than large-scale construction. The researchers aim to incorporate solar-powered blocks into the SparkBlocks range of children’s educational kits, potentially replacing the battery packs currently used to power electronic components.

“We expect the first iteration to appear as solar energy blocks for use in the SparkBlocks portfolio in children’s educational kits, replacing the battery packs in the current kits, on relatively short terms,” Van Best stated.

Once the researchers have gained more experience with manufacturing and performance, they plan to explore scaling the technology to architectural brick-like dimensions. Such developments could eventually support the integration of colourful solar-harvesting elements into buildings and public infrastructure, although no commercial deployment timetable has been established.

“The eventual application and integration of LSC systems will be best initiated by a creative artistic mind, and I look forward to see what such creative persons will come up with,” Van Best concluded.

According to recent reports, luminescent solar concentrators have been investigated for a range of applications, including solar windows, agrivoltaic systems and greenhouses, and bifacial PV installations. Researchers from the University of Twente found that free-space LSCs could increase winter electricity generation by up to 60% and annual energy yield by 12% compared with conventional monofacial systems.

Industry observers note that researchers at Eindhoven University of Technology have also explored LSC technology in previous studies. In 2021, a TU/e research team developed measurement protocols to standardize the characterization of LSC devices and support their commercial development. In 2022, a Dutch-Australian research group involving TU/e scientists developed cubical LSC devices equipped with bifacial silicon solar cells for urban applications, with the best-performing configuration achieving a power conversion efficiency of 11.6%.

Chilean PV plant hit by cyberattack remains disconnected

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the 103 MW Huatacondo solar plant and its 98 MW/312 MWh battery energy storage system (BESS), located in Chile’s Tarapacá region, remain disconnected from the national grid nearly three months after a cyberattack in August, as pv magazine reported on Oct.
  • 11, Chilean lawmaker Cristián Araya Lerdo de Tejada submitted two formal requests for information to the ministries of Public Security and Energy, seeking clarification on the circumstances surrounding the incident and the measures taken in response.
  • According to recent reports, according to the Coordinator’s daily report for Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the 103 MW Huatacondo solar plant and its 98 MW/312 MWh battery energy storage system (BESS), located in Chile’s Tarapacá region, remain disconnected from the national grid nearly three months after a cyberattack in August, as pv magazine reported on Oct. 28. Chile’s National Electric Coordinator (Coordinador Eléctrico Nacional) has confirmed that it activated disconnection protocols to protect the grid and that an investigation remains ongoing.

It has been revealed that on Nov. 11, Chilean lawmaker Cristián Araya Lerdo de Tejada submitted two formal requests for information to the ministries of Public Security and Energy, seeking clarification on the circumstances surrounding the incident and the measures taken in response.

According to recent reports, according to the Coordinator’s daily report for Nov. 14, both the solar plant and the BESS had 0% availability and remained listed as forced disconnections. The report cites the same cause recorded on Aug. 27, under forced disconnection request SDCF 2026100475, attributing the outage to a cyberattack targeting the Huatacondo facilities. The BESS is still undergoing commissioning, meaning its unavailability does not constitute an interruption of commercial operations.

In comments reported by Chilean broadcaster T13, Patricio Leyton, cybersecurity director at the National Electric Coordinator, stated the organization activated its disconnection protocol to safeguard the electricity system after receiving information from the affected company.

In a recent development, the Coordinator described the incident as exceptional and remarked it continues to receive updates on the investigation, but declined to provide further details, citing confidentiality. T13 dated the attack to Aug. 26, while the Coordinator’s operational records show that a disconnection request was filed on Aug. 27.

In a recent development, the T13 report also stated two other suspected cyberattacks involving facilities in the Coquimbo region had subsequently been ruled out. On Aug. 27, the Coordinator’s records attributed the loss of monitoring and remote-control capabilities at the Olivos and Espinos thermal power plants in Los Vilos to a cyberattack.

In a recent development, this represents a development from the account published by pv magazine on Oct. 28, although no independent documentary confirmation of the dismissal of those incidents has been found. On the same day, a forced disconnection was also requested for the 220/23 kV TR1 transformer at the Santa Rita substation, with a cyberattack cited as the cause.

Against this backdrop, Araya submitted two formal requests for information through the Chamber of Deputies, numbered 28298 and 28300.

The first, addressed to the Ministry of Public Security, asks the National Cybersecurity Agency (ANCI) to provide information on the incidents and verify whether the companies operating the affected facilities, as well as the Coordinator, complied with the notification requirements under Chile’s Framework Cybersecurity Law.

The law requires an initial alert within three hours of becoming aware of an incident with a potentially significant impact, an update within 72 hours and a final report within 15 calendar days.

The second request, addressed to the Ministry of Energy, seeks clarification on whether the incidents’ cyber-related origins have been technically confirmed, whether any connection between them has been established and which systems were compromised.

It specifically refers to supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) systems, remote-control equipment, electrical protection systems, inverters and BESS management systems.

The request also seeks information on potential unauthorized remote access, the operational and economic impact of the incident, preventive measures implemented at other renewable energy and storage facilities, and the expected timeline for reconnecting the Huatacondo plant.

Araya also requested an upgrade on the Technical Standard for Cybersecurity and Information Security for the electricity sector, which Chile’s National Energy Commission submitted for public consultation in August.

Recent findings suggest that as of Nov. 16, the Chamber of Deputies had recorded no response to either request. No technical findings have been publicly released regarding the origin of the Huatacondo cyberattack, the specific systems affected or a confirmed date for the resumption of operations at the solar plant and its battery storage system.

  • In a recent development, for utility-scale PV projects, the DC collection network influences both construction efficiency and long-term connection reliability.
  • Industry observers note that at RE+, SUNKEAN officially introduced its ETL-certified 2000 VDC TRUNK-TTM system, extending its pre-assembled collection portfolio to higher-voltage applications.
  • Recent findings suggest that TRUNK-TTM supports customized configurations to accommodate string positions, equipment locations, and project-specific layouts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, for utility-scale PV projects, the DC collection network influences both construction efficiency and long-term connection reliability. Across large arrays, cable routing and repeated wiring operations require careful coordination. SUNKEAN addresses these challenges through two product groups: factory-assembled trunk systems and PV wire harnesses.

Industry observers note that at RE+, SUNKEAN officially introduced its ETL-certified 2000 VDC TRUNK-TTM system, extending its pre-assembled collection portfolio to higher-voltage applications. Designed for large ground-mounted solar plants, the system integrates trunk cables and branch connections into a single assembly that collects DC power from PV strings and delivers it to a disconnect box.

Recent findings suggest that TRUNK-TTM supports customized configurations to accommodate string positions, equipment locations, and project-specific layouts. Its vertical cable exits facilitate branch cable routing, helping installers follow the planned collection layout. Factory pre-assembly reduces the number of individual connection tasks performed on site, helping standardize connection work across the array.

The system’s current collection architecture addresses a separate concern: localized temperature rise. Where several branch currents converge directly at one point on the trunk conductor, this concentration of current can lead to localized heating. TRUNK-TTM instead uses a staged approach, combining incoming branch currents before feeding the combined current into the trunk cable. This design is intended to reduce the risk of excessive localized temperature rise.

SUNKEAN also offers copper-to-aluminum and all-aluminum options, giving customers greater flexibility to select conductors in line with the project’s electrical design and material requirements.

Alongside its trunk system, SUNKEAN offers PV wire harnesses with multiple branch configurations, including S-Y, S-X, and S-T designs, to accommodate different module layouts. Factory assembly helps reduce connection errors and maintain consistent installation quality. Matching the harness configuration to the module layout before construction also helps contractors prepare for installation.

Sources indicate that for EPC contractors, the combined portfolio helps blueprint wiring assemblies around the project layout and better manage on-site workloads. For developers, it offers a way to balance construction costs with the need for reliable DC connections throughout the plant’s operating life.

In a recent development, SUNKEAN’s product innovations reflect its commitment to advancing solar connectivity. By addressing both construction needs and connection performance, the manufacturer aims to help customers build more reliable PV systems that support stable, long-term operation and greater sustainability.

German companies develop safety concept for inverter-free plug-in battery storage

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Indielux GmbH, a developer of plug-in solar and storage safety technology, and p&e power&energy GmbH, a specialist in battery power electronics, have signed a memorandum of understanding to implement a jointly developed safety concept for modular plug-in battery storage systems.
  • The concept combines p&e’s multilevel technology, which generates alternating current (AC) directly at the battery cell level without a central inverter, with Indielux’s patented ready2plugin safety technology.
  • According to recent reports, according to the companies, this is particularly key for plug-in storage systems installed in living spaces or on balconies, where stringent safety requirements apply.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Indielux GmbH, a developer of plug-in solar and storage safety technology, and p&e power&energy GmbH, a specialist in battery power electronics, have signed a memorandum of understanding to implement a jointly developed safety concept for modular plug-in battery storage systems.

The concept combines p&e’s multilevel technology, which generates alternating current (AC) directly at the battery cell level without a central inverter, with Indielux’s patented ready2plugin safety technology. The companies say the combination is designed to prevent household electrical wiring from overheating.

According to recent reports, according to the companies, this is particularly key for plug-in storage systems installed in living spaces or on balconies, where stringent safety requirements apply. Conventional circuit breakers typically detect current drawn from the grid but do not account for additional power fed into household circuits by storage systems. This can cause wiring to overheat and damage PVC insulation.

“If a storage system continuously feeds an additional 800 W into the circuit, the wiring could reach a critical state in just about six months. At 2,500 W, the wiring becomes so hot that the insulation begins to decompose, posing a fire hazard,” the companies mentioned.

In a recent development, indielux’s ready2plugin technology monitors electrical circuits in real time and disconnects the power supply before the wiring overheats. According to the manufacturer, the maximum amount of electricity that can be fed into a household circuit through a standard socket without additional overload protection is 1,200 kWh per year. With ready2plugin, that figure can increase to as much as 22,800 kWh per year, according to the company.

In a recent development, P&e’s power electronics platform incorporates a dedicated switching stage for each battery cell, allowing the system to switch voltages of just a few volts rather than several hundred volts. The architecture eliminates the need for a central inverter, enables weaker cells to be bypassed and minimizes switching losses. According to p&e, the power electronics achieve efficiency levels exceeding 99%. Under moderate loads, the modules require no cooling fan and can also be installed outdoors, depending on the battery chemistry and enclosure design.

“Plug-in storage systems are becoming increasingly powerful, yet the household electrical wiring remains the same,” stated Marcus Vietzke, managing director of Indielux. “That is why circuit protection must be integrated into every module from the very start. The concept is set. Now, we are building the safest and most efficient plug-in storage system.”.

The companies initiative to begin by testing the integration of ready2plugin technology into p&e’s storage systems. Under the proposed design, each module will function as a standalone storage unit, with a capacity of 2 kWh to 5 kWh, an output of up to 2.3 kW and integrated grid and circuit protection.

In a recent development, multiple modules will be able to feed up to 2.6 kW into a household circuit through a single socket. In the event of a grid outage, the companies say the integrated emergency power outlets will provide a combined output of up to 4.6 kW.

The jointly developed safety concept includes 24 technical measures aimed at meeting VDE standards for personal safety, electrical wiring protection and grid protection.

The guide offers considerations applicable to different climate regions, but it is framed by IGAD in the context of preparedness, anticipatory action and resilience in the Horn of Africa (Djibouti, Eritrea, Ethiopia, Kenya, Somalia, South Sudan, Sudan and Uganda). Its aim is to offer actionable guidance to improve urban resilience, protect vulnerable communities and reduce the impacts of climate-related hazards.

According to recent reports, the guide, "El Niño Preparedness: An Anticipatory Action Framework for City Leaders," is grounded in two premises: that urban preparedness is a governance function, and that climate forecasts can be translated into local action at the scale of cities and municipal governments. From ICPAC's perspective, the value of a climate forecast lies in the action it enables by triggering solid protocols ahead of El Niño-driven rains. The guide encourages cities to use the forecast lead time to make decisions on the ground and turn early warnings into early action. The document proposes a protocol structure and checklists to translate climate forecasts into risk information based on pre-agreed thresholds. Triggered preventive actions include administrative measures, such as releasing funding and warning households, and practical measures, such as clearing drains and pre-positioning emergency supplies.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The National Museum of Norway has announced Painted Matter as the title of Norway's contribution to the 20th International Architecture Exhibition of the Venice Biennale, scheduled to take place from May 8 to November 21, 2027. Developed by Oslo-based practice Kastler Skjeseth Architects, the exhibition will be presented at the Nordic Pavilion and will explore the role of traditional decorative painting techniques in contemporary architecture, with a focus on material use, architectural expression, and sustainability. The Nordic Pavilion, designed by Norwegian architect Sverre Fehn, is jointly owned by Norway, Sweden, and Finland. For the 2027 edition, the National Museum of Norway is responsible for organizing the Nordic contribution on behalf of Moderna Museet in Stockholm and the Architecture and Design Museum in Helsinki.

The project will further investigate questions of authenticity and material value. The exhibition will explore how these distinctions inform perceptions of authenticity and status in architecture, including how the value assigned to materials changes over time.

In a recent development, through these practices, Painted Matter will examine the relationship between traditional craftsmanship and contemporary approaches to construction. The exhibition connects the reuse of existing materials and the consideration of material life cycles with renewed interest in ornament, historical references, and architectural expression. It also considers how decorative painting can transform existing surfaces without requiring the introduction of latest materials, bringing traditional techniques into discussions around material scarcity and environmental awareness. Latest Update: Winston Churchill Desperately Wanted a Wartime Meeting With FDR. He Got It, and Their Three-Week Christmas Summit Changed the Trajectory of WWII

💡 Key Takeaways

  • One of Churchill’s personal secretaries, Kathleen Hill, sat in the corner, trying, as she always did when the prime minister was upset, to be invisible.
  • As first lord of the Admiralty in two world wars and now as prime minister, Churchill loved battleships.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that on the morning of December 10, 1941, Winston Churchill finished his massive breakfast in bed at No. 10 Downing Street, as was his custom, and opened his red box of official business. The telephone at his bedside rang. Admiral Dudley Pound, the first sea lord, was calling, but Churchill could not quite hear what he was saying. “His voice sounded odd,” Churchill later wrote. Then the words came clearly: The Japanese had sunk both the battleship Prince of Wales and the battle cruiser Repulse in the South China Sea, where the ships had been tasked with securing Britain’s Far East interests. “We think by aircraft,” noted Pound. He also told Churchill that Tom Phillips, the task force commander and a close friend of the prime minister, had drowned. “Are you sure it’s true?” asked Churchill. “No doubt at all,” the admiral said.

One of Churchill’s personal secretaries, Kathleen Hill, sat in the corner, trying, as she always did when the prime minister was upset, to be invisible. Churchill put down the phone and was now twisting in bed. “Poor Tom Phillips,” he moaned, and for the next two days, when he thought no one was watching, he wept and mumbled to himself, “I don’t understand what happened. I don’t understand.”.

As first lord of the Admiralty in two world wars and now as prime minister, Churchill loved battleships. He counted on these magnificent “castles of steel,” as he called them, to secure Britain’s centuries-long mastery of the seas. They “can catch and kill anything,” he regularly boasted. But Churchill was mourning more than the loss of a friend and two capital ships.

Sources indicate that when, just three days before, Japan had attacked the American naval base at Pearl Harbor on December 7, bringing America into the war, Churchill had felt immensely relieved. Years later in his memoirs he would write that on that night, he “slept the sleep of the saved.” His relief, as it turned out, was premature. For months, the British prime minister had been imploring U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt to ask Congress for a declaration of war on Germany. But on December 8, the morning after Pearl Harbor, Roosevelt asked Congress to declare war against Japan—not, to Churchill’s alarm, against Germany as well. Now, with the sinking of Britain’s two great warships in the Pacific, the British crown colonies of Hong Kong and Singapore were exposed to Japanese attack. And Churchill still had no assurance that the United States would join Britain in the battle against Nazi fascism.

As always, the prime minister collected himself. He knew that he must rise and do his duty. Before lunch, Churchill addressed a sullen and worried House of Commons. One of his more biting critics, the American­-born Conservative Member of Parliament Henry Channon, was unsparing that night in his diary:.

A dreadful day of despair and despondency. The prime minister stalked into the House and seemed anxious to speak. ... He declared the sinking of both the Prince of Wales and the Repulse at Malaya. A most shattering blow for our Pacific fleet and naval prestige. ... A wave of gloom spread everywhere.

Churchill’s first stop after the gloom in Parliament was to see the U.S. ambassador, John Winant. Churchill wanted to travel across the Atlantic to plead with Roosevelt face-to-face not to devote all of America’s resources to fight Japan. Right after the Pearl Harbor attack, Washington suspended its lend-lease program supplying war materials to Britain. Now the prime minister worried that, along with its two magnificent frontline warships, Britain might lose the crucial munitions and supplies it needed from America to keep fighting. Churchill put on his bulldog face. The dire news of the sinkings of Britain’s main warships in the Pacific, he told Winant, was even more reason for Churchill and Roosevelt to meet and strategy the way forward—and to do it right away. As Winant knew, what Churchill really wanted, and what still eluded him, was a declaration of war by America against Germany.

Historian Evan Thomas vividly takes readers into the war rooms of Roosevelt, Churchill and Hitler as they redefined the world.

The U.S. ambassador was deeply sympathetic to Britain and personally close to Churchill. (He was also having an extramarital affair with Churchill’s daughter Sarah.) In his report back to Washington, Winant did his diplomatic best to dress up Churchill’s desperation, saying that “discouragement seems only to give him new courage and add to his determination.” Churchill’s courage was real; there was no other virtue that he prized more, especially in trying circumstances like the loss of the Prince of Wales. His army chief of staff, General Alan Brooke, noted in his diary that the prime minister had “stood [the] shock well.” But Brooke also observed that Churchill was “fretting” at Roosevelt’s delaying tactics.

The American president was, as usual, biding his time. With one eye, Roosevelt was warily watching Congress and especially the non-interventionist America First movement and its champion, the hero aviator Charles Lindbergh, who had dropped their opposition to America going to war with Japan, but fighting Germany was another matter. The popular Senator Hiram Johnson, a devout isolationist from California, had used his power as ranking Republican on the Foreign Relations Committee to halt legislation intended to prepare an American Expeditionary Force for action in Europe within the next two years. (Johnson told his son that he had at least ten other senators on his side.).

The day before, Roosevelt put off Churchill’s proposal to come to America by suggesting that the voyage through U-­boat-infested waters was too dangerous. On the evening of December 10, Churchill brushed aside any temporizing. In a secret cable, he wrote Roosevelt, “We do not think there is any serious danger about return journey. There is, however, great danger in our not having a full discussion on the highest level about the extreme gravity of the naval position [the sunken American and British ships], as well as upon all the production and allocation complications involved [lend-lease, now on hold]. I am quite ready to meet you at Bermuda or to fly from Bermuda to Washington. I feel it would be disastrous to wait for another month.”.

In Washington, where it was just after lunch, Roosevelt continued to stall. He, too, had been shocked by the British setbacks in the Far East, and he wished both to commiserate with Churchill and to keep his distance. Summoning his secretary Grace Tully, he began to dictate a message using Churchill’s favorite appellation, “For Former Naval Person from the President:”.

I would like to suggest delay in decision reference to conference until early stages of mobilization complete here and situation in Pacific more clarified. ...

Sources indicate that he finished drafting the message, but he didn’t send it. He knew that Churchill was deathly afraid that America would mobilize all its resources to fight Japan and abandon its “Germany First” strategy, which had been settled on almost a year earlier. More recently, it was fleshed out in a planning document, the Victory Program, which called for an invasion of Europe by five million American men in 1943. Roosevelt himself had not abandoned Germany First. He said as much in his “fireside chat” radio address just the night before, even telling Americans that Adolf Hitler was the true instigator of the Pearl Harbor attack. Roosevelt believed that the gravest threat to world freedom was from Nazi Germany, not Imperial Japan. But he was leery of getting ahead of Congress and inadvertently fanning the embers of America First, which seemed to be rapidly evolving into Japan First.

Roosevelt summoned Tully and started over:.

I know you understand why it is impossible for me to leave Washington until January sixth. We are in the throes of mobilization and the preparations for the new Congress ...

It has been revealed that he didn’t send that draft, either. Instinctively, he was waiting for a sign, some indication of what Hitler intended to do. Would Hitler join the fight on the side of Japan? American code-breakers had been reading Japan’s diplomatic cables, and they suggested that Germany would be willing to support Japan in a war against America. If Hitler declared war, then Roosevelt would not need to be the one to persuade Congress. Hitler would have done it for him.

Months before the December 1941 attack on Pearl Harbor, Roosevelt and Churchill held a secret meeting of alliance.

In August, the leaders drafted the Atlantic Charter, an agreement outlining how the world would look after the war was won.

Churchill and Roosevelt conducted their business on a warship, anchored in Canadian waters.

It has been revealed that A report from Roosevelt’s chief of intelligence, Colonel William Donovan, arrived that afternoon confirming Roosevelt’s hunch. It stated that the German government had told a German newspaperman working in Washington to leave as soon as possible for Europe or South America, because Germany was about to declare war on the United States. Though he was not privy to Hitler’s thoughts, the German newspaperman recited to Roosevelt’s spymaster the führer’s doomed logic: “Germany would rather declare war on the United States than wait for the United States to declare war on her—this for the reason that she wishes to show her people her internal strength.”.

Industry observers note that then, shortly before 6 p.m. came official word from the German government that Hitler would make a major address the next day. Some American news accounts, lacking Roosevelt’s intelligence sources but feeding off rumors, speculated that Hitler had summoned his government to declare war on America.

The hour was striking. At 6:30 in the evening, Roosevelt asked Tully to take a message:.

For Former Naval Person from the President:.

Delighted to have you here at the White House ...

During the early afternoon of December 11, crowds began to gather outside the Kroll Opera House, near the burnt-out Reichstag building in the heart of Berlin. Dignitaries had gathered from the far reaches of the Reich to hear Hitler’s speech. There was Norway’s prime minister, Vidkun Quisling, whose name was becoming synonymous with “collaborator,” and Amin al-Husseini, the former grand mufti of Jerusalem. An honor guard of the panzer division Leibstandarte SS Adolf Hitler, an elite SS unit formed from Hitler’s bodyguards, arrived in their all­-black uniforms with silver SS lightning bolts pinned on their collars. They awaited the SS commander, Heinrich Himmler, who designed their showy uniforms. Always attentive to detail, Himmler had gone to the hairdresser the day before.

Recent findings suggest that as Nazi officialdom arrived at the opera house, Foreign Minister Joachim von Ribbentrop was still at his office on Wilhelmstrasse, where he had summoned the American chargé d’affaires, Leland Morris. At 2:15 p.m., Ribbentrop read a statement declaring that “Germany, too, as from today, considers herself as being in a state of war with the United States of America.” With an operatic touch, the foreign minister concluded his presentation by telling the American diplomat, “Your president wanted war. Now, he has it.”.

In Washington, meanwhile, the German chargé, Hans Thomsen, was kept cooling his heels for 90 minutes at the U.S. State Department before he could deliver the same message to a midlevel official, who was finally sent out to the waiting room to receive him. Emerging from the building into a chilly, overcast December morning, Thomsen, who had requested safe passage home to Germany, turned to the gaggle of reporters and inquired, “Anybody want to buy a nice car?”.

Back in Berlin, just before 3 p.m., Hitler and Himmler arrived in a massive Mercedes­-Benz limousine. Hitler inspected the honor guard while a band played the “Horst-Wessel-Lied,” the marching song that was the Nazi Party anthem. Hitler chose to address the nation in midafternoon so his speech could be heard both in Japan, where it was 11 p.m., and Washington, where it was 9 a.m.

At the podium, Hitler stood before a giant gold eagle clutching a swastika in its claw. His tone was somber but self-righteous. “The American president and his plutocratic clique have mocked us as the ‘have-nots,’” he said. “That is correct!” He went on to contrast himself with Roosevelt. The American president came from “a rich family.” Hitler came from nothing. While Roosevelt avoided military service in World War I, Hitler was an “ordinary soldier.” But now the Reich, the people and their führer were one and the same, locked in a relentless but ultimately victorious struggle against communism, capitalism and—always—“the eternal Jew,” a term  popularized in a Nazi propaganda film.

A journalist from neutral Sweden, Arvid Fredborg, was watching and taking notes. The officials from the Foreign Office and the Propaganda Ministry were, he reported, applauding, but mechanically, ritualistically. Some appeared uneasy, glancing at each other when Hitler “screamed out his hatred for the American president—the ‘cripple’—and his wife.” During one round of orchestrated applause, Fredborg looked down a line of field marshals, generals and admirals and saw “not a single hand move.”.

It has been revealed that after 90 increasingly histrionic minutes, Hitler declared war on America and left the building. “Sieg Heil!” shouted the Reichstag deputies.

In a recent development, all day long, a trainload of 1,000 Jews made its way across Germany, headed eastward, into the conquered lands of Eastern Europe, to slave factories and crematoria. The “transport” began in the rain at 4 a.m., after the Jews were herded from a slaughterhouse in Düsseldorf, where they had been rounded up for the night, into the railroad boxcars that would take them ... where? They were not told.

Recent findings suggest that the world was now officially at war. The Allies (the United States, Britain and its Commonwealth, China, and the Soviet Union) arrayed against the Axis (the German and Japanese Empires, Italy, and their various vassal states) in the largest and deadliest conflict in the history of mankind.

In a recent development, in Washington, hours after Thomsen delivered Germany’s declaration of war on America, Roosevelt did not mention Hitler’s name when he sent a message to Congress calling for war with Germany. Congress needed no persuasion. Not even the determined pacifist Jeannette Rankin of Montana voted no; instead, she voted “present.” At its Chicago headquarters, the America First organization officially dissolved.

According to recent reports, this was the moment that Roosevelt had been patiently waiting for and, sometimes secretly, planning for. To be sure, he had taken crucial steps on the road to war, authorizing massive ship-building programs, including the creation of a “two-ocean navy”; enabling conscription and directing American military planners to meet clandestinely with their British counterparts. In a move little remarked upon at the time, in June 1941, he had signed an executive order banning racial discrimination by defense contractors, opening the way for the assembly lines in Detroit to be integrated. But, always, Roosevelt had been mindful of political reality, that an American president cannot get too far ahead of his people.

Now, the equivocations were over. The mighty American industrial base would go to work, around the clock, making more tanks, planes and ships than Germany and Japan could dream of. Their fates were sealed.

In London, one of Churchill’s private secretaries, John Martin, wrote in his diary, “The stars in their courses are fighting for us.” He was quoting Churchill quoting the Bible (Judges 5:20: “They fought from heaven, the stars in their courses ...”). Another private secretary, John Peck, wrote a friend that despite the loss of the Prince of Wales, Churchill was “full of bounce again.”.

Industry observers note that still, for all the giddiness at No. 10 Downing Street that America was finally in the fight, the mood in Parliament earlier that day had been oddly subdued, Harold Nicolson, a junior minister, wrote his wife. “We simply can’t be beaten with America in,” he wrote. “But how strange it is that this great event should be recorded and welcomed here without any jubilation. We should have gone mad with joy if it had happened a year ago. ... Not an American flag flying in the whole of London. How odd we are!”.

Londoners, perhaps, were a little resentful that the Americans had stayed out of the fray for so long while they suffered. They also knew that the suffering was far from over. Churchill had told them so in a speech to Parliament that morning, warning of “heavy punishment” ahead.

On December 12, Churchill gathered with most of his military service chiefs of staff and his secretaries, a party of 38 people, on a train platform at Euston Station in London. The cover story was that they had come to see off Max Aitken, the minister of production, on his way to Scotland to board a ship for Washington. Actually, they were all going across the ocean. It had taken Churchill less than 24 hours from the time he received Roosevelt’s message—“Delighted to have you here at the White House”—to gather his entourage for the perilous voyage to America, scheduled to take seven days zigzagging through U-boat hunting grounds at 20 knots.

Churchill was in a puckish mood. When one of his military chiefs warned him to be cautious about asking things of the Americans, his face lit up with a wicked leer. “Oh, that is the way we talked to her when we were wooing her,” he said. “Now that she is in the harem, we talk to her quite differently.”.

It has been revealed that the battleship carrying Churchill and his party was the Duke of York, the brand-new sister ship of the late Prince of Wales. The Admiralty sent the Duke of York from Scotland down through the Irish Sea across shipping lanes patrolled by German bombers flying out of bases on the west coast of France. Stepping out on the bridge, Churchill saw “unwelcome blue sky” through the clouds. He could not help but think of the hard­-learned lesson of air power and the fate of the Prince of Wales.

It was winter, and the North Atlantic raged. Giant waves crashed over the bow. Everyone was trapped in stuffy compartments below deck. Churchill took an extra dose of Mothersill’s Travel Remedy to fight off seasickness and, in a long letter to Clementine, his wife, he paraphrased the 18th-century writer Samuel Johnson: “Being in a ship in such weather as this is like being in a prison, with the extra chance of being drowned.” Aitken joked over dinner, which had few takers, that he had never traveled in such a large submarine.

The weather was so bad that the Duke of York’s destroyer escorts, tossed about like bathtub toys, could not keep up. The battleship pressed on alone. In the dark storm­-tossed night, the captain assured Churchill that the ship was more likely to ram a German U­-boat than be sighted and sunk by one.

In his tender letter to Clementine—“my darling”—with whom he freely discussed state secrets in a way Roosevelt never would with his wife, Eleanor, he worried about how he would be received by the Americans. “Oddly enough,” he wrote, “we have got practically nothing from the United States wireless. I do not, therefore, know the situation I shall find on arrival.”.

For days, he lay in bed, reading cables about the uneven progress of the war and trying to restore his profoundly weary body. “The entry of the United States into the war is worth all the losses sustained in the East many times over,” he wrote his wife. But the sinking of the Prince of Wales and the imminent fall of Hong Kong were “painful to endure and will be very hard to repair.” At sea, the storms raged on. “It is still blowing hard, and from my porthole I can see, every minute, tremendous seas pouring over the bows of the ship,” he wrote.

Still, he made the most of his passage. He drafted long memos on strategy for his chiefs of staff, as well as for Roosevelt and Joseph Stalin, the Soviet dictator who had become an ally in June when Hitler invaded Russia; he read a novel about a naval hero; and, his sea legs under him, he prowled the passageways. At night there were melodramatic movies to watch. He was enthralled by The Sea Hawk, a 1940 swashbuckling adventure film starring Errol Flynn that was lightly disguised pro-British propaganda. Dressed in his beloved silk dressing gown, festooned with Chinese dragons, the prime minister jumped from his chair before the makeshift movie screen when the underdog English seamen, circa 1600, rose up with swords and pikes against their Spanish oppressors. “We’re winning! We’re winning!” Churchill cried.

According to recent reports, on December 22, two days behind schedule because of the rough seas, the Duke of York put in at Norfolk, Virginia. The plan had been to steam up the Chesapeake Bay and then travel along the Potomac River to Washington. He had wanted to make a grand entrance to show that the Royal Navy might have lost the Prince of Wales, but there would always be a Duke of York to replace the fallen. But Churchill was in too much of a hurry. He commandeered a two­-engine Lockheed plane at the American Navy base. After flying through the darkness for three-quarters of an hour, the British visitors saw the lights of the American capital all ablaze. (There were blackout curtains at the White House and a few other federal buildings, but nowhere else.).

According to recent reports, after the gloom of blacked-out London, they were deeply moved. “One of the most beautiful sights I have ever seen,” John Martin wrote in his diary. Churchill’s aide-de-camp, Commander Tommy Thompson, could not get over the “amazing spectacle of a whole city all lighted up.” Thompson wrote, “Washington represented something immensely precious. Freedom, hope, strength. We had not seen an illuminated city for five years. My heart filled.”.

It has been revealed that when the plane landed, a tall man greeted them: Franklin D. Roosevelt. Churchill would write in his memoirs, “I clasped his strong hand with comfort and pleasure.”.

Recent findings suggest that first lady Eleanor Roosevelt was understandably annoyed at her husband, who had not told her until that very morning, December 22, that the prime minister of Great Britain was coming to America and would be staying at the White House. In the December 24 installment of her confiding and chatty syndicated newspaper column, “My Day,” she complained to her millions of readers. In any event, he knew, based on long experience, that she would rise to the occasion.

Industry observers note that the news of her houseguest’s imminent arrival made Eleanor late for her appointments. Always, she was in a hurry. After a morning press conference, she headed to the Salvation Army, then to the American Committee for British Catholic Relief and finally to a tree lighting sponsored by the Washington Federation of Churches. At 6:15 p.m., she was back at the White House to welcome the prime minister.

He was not an easy guest. In the morning, with his bare feet sticking out from his long underwear, the British prime minister addressed the president’s butler, Alonzo Fields. “Now, Fields,” he began, in a friendly way but leaving no doubt about his needs: “One, I don’t like talking outside my quarters; two, I hate whistling in the corridors; and three, I must have a tumbler of sherry in my room before breakfast.” He went on, asking for Scotch and soda before lunch, and champagne and 90-year-old brandy before bed.

In a recent development, war had come, and the military delegations of both nations worked in concert night and day for the next three weeks. But it was the Christmas season, and time for one of Roosevelt’s favorite ceremonies, the Christmas Eve lighting of the National Christmas Tree. The president loved trees, and for many years he had been growing and selling Christmas trees at his estate in Hyde Park. He even identified his occupation as “tree farmer” when he registered to vote. He delighted in the annual ceremony, which he had moved from the Ellipse to the White House grounds to make it a more “homey” celebration. Notwithstanding Secret Service jitters, thousands of people passed through inspections at the gates to gather near the fence on the South Lawn, where the stately, live 30-foot spruce was decorated in red, white and blue lights. Watching from the South Portico of the White House, Eleanor stood with Churchill and Norway’s Crown Princess Märtha, a close friend of the president; Märtha’s young children; and her husband, Crown Prince Olav, whom Roosevelt had brought to Washington to spend Christmas with his family.

The president turned the switch, and the tree glowed with a thousand little bulbs. As the darkness of war pressed in, he asked the people throughout the nation to prepare their hearts and light their Christmas candles, conscious of the sacrifices ahead. (The tree was not lit again until December 1945.).

Then it was Churchill’s turn to speak.

In a recent development, “This is a strange Christmas Eve,” the prime minister noted. “Almost the whole world is locked in deadly struggle.” But it was still Christmas, a time for remembering the promise of love and peace. “Here, then, for one night only,” intoned the familiar bulldog voice, “each home throughout the English-speaking world should be a brightly lighted island of happiness and peace.” Recalling centuries of shared tradition, Churchill went on:.

Let the children have their night of fun and laughter. Let the gifts of Father Christmas delight their play. Let us grown-ups share to the full in their unstinted pleasures before we turn again to the stern task and the formidable years that lie before us, resolved that, by our sacrifice and daring, these same children shall not be robbed of their inheritance or denied their right to live in a free and decent world.

Industry observers note that unfailingly, Churchill spoke of light against the dark. He had come from blacked-out London to the now bright-lit warmth of the White House portico with a message of hope. Churchill and the American president standing beside him, his withered legs straightened by steel braces, summoned the forces of light—for freedom from tyranny and for basic human decency. Across the ocean, Hitler stood for the forces of darkness.

This article is a selection from the December 2026 issue of Smithsonian magazine.

Indeed, in Hitler’s Germany that night, there was little sign of Christmas. Germans, denied their yuletide present-giving, were dutifully sending their hats, coats and woolens to soldiers freezing to death at the Russian front. As Hitler imagined the future, the only cross to be revered in the Reich would be the iron cross of Nazism. Fed lies about the splendors of National Socialism, the German people had to line up to buy rationed cigarettes. (Men got the equivalent of 1¾ smokes per day, women half that.).

In his nightly dinner rants, Hitler had spoken of a grandiose new civilization—its lands crisscrossed by gleaming highways—controlled by monumental party headquarters in a reimagined Berlin. Meanwhile, his nominal successor, Reich Marshal Hermann Göring, had been looting treasures from nations under the Nazi yoke. The week before Pearl Harbor, Göring had idled his time appropriating centuries of art from the Jeu de Paume in Paris, from the museums of Antwerp and Amsterdam, and from Jewish homes, for the Reich’s new museums but also for his hunting lodge. Later in the war, Göring would appear before guests dressed in a toga, as if he were a Roman demigod, instead of the failed chief of the Luftwaffe.

Industry observers note that hitler’s aides—Göring, Ribbentrop, Joseph Goebbels and all the rest—were, for all their swagger, small men obsessed with the trappings of power and greed. They were fated, by the laws of God and nature reaching back to antiquity, to self-destruct.

Sources indicate that and yet destiny was not obvious in the moment. Just six months earlier, in July of 1941, it really had appeared that the Third Reich would take Russia, that the Empire of Japan would conquer Asia, that fascism would rule the world, or a good deal of it. In early December, Hitler’s tanks had reached the gates of Moscow while Japanese planes, ships and soldiers were marching and killing from Singapore to Honolulu.

Then, suddenly but inexorably, the tide turned.

Churchill spent three weeks living on the second floor of the White House in the Rose Room (also known as the Queen’s Bedroom), with his secretaries working across the hall in Abraham Lincoln’s private sitting room. “We live here as a big family,” Churchill wired Clement Attlee, head of the opposition Labour Party in England. Late into the wee hours, Roosevelt and Churchill smoked and drank and discussed the war. Eleanor gave Churchill a bit of knowing advice, born of experience: “You know, Winston, when Franklin says ‘yes, yes, yes,’ it doesn’t mean he agrees with you. It means he’s listening.” Her caution was understandable. The two men were partners, not yet true friends, and their journey would be long and winding and not without its setbacks and disappointments. But they had begun. Working together, officials from the two nations created a joint military command and began plotting the steps toward the liberation of Europe.

Sources indicate that on the day after Christmas, Churchill addressed a Joint Session of Congress. He inveighed against the tyranny of the Nazis and the brutal aggression of the Japanese. “What kind of a people do they think we are?” he asked, indignant, his voice rising. “Is it possible they do not realize that we shall never cease to persevere against them until they have been taught a lesson which they and the world will never forget?”.

Sources indicate that it was a war cry, and the senators and congressmen roared their approval, raising their fingers in the V-for-Victory salute. But when Churchill asked What kind of a people do they think we are? he did not mean just fighters. His unspoken message was that they are also the kind of people who believed in a world that could be free and just, where its people were decent and good.

Evan Thomas is a former correspondent for Time and Washington bureau chief for Newsweek.

Industry News: Revealed: Russia, Saudi Arabia and Australia are largest CO2 exporters of all time
