📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the Indonesian province of West Kalimantan, on the island of Borneo, is no stranger to wildfires. Horrific wildfires burned in 2015 and 2019, the latter of which set ablaze around 1.6 million hectares of Indonesian forest and land. However, the scale of destruction from this year’s El Niño-intensified fires throughout the island is unprecedented, according to the nonprofit International Animal Rescue.

In a recent development, earlier this year, four mother-baby orangutan pairs and one adult female orangutan (genus Pongo) were rescued from areas in Ketapang (a regency in the West Kalimantan province) impacted by the fires. They were dehydrated and malnourished, and some had burned their feet, likely because they stepped on embers as they crossed burning peatland.

Recent findings suggest that they were taken to an orangutan rescue and rehabilitation centre in Ketapang, West Kalimantan. The center is run by Yayasan Inisiasi Alam Rehabilitasi Indonesia (YIARI), a nonprofit dedicated to primate and habitat conservation in Indonesia. YIARI’s medical team kept an eye on their recovery, and then conducted health examinations to make sure they were all ready for release. The last of these examinations revealed that three of the females were pregnant.

“Their return to the wild is therefore especially key, giving these mothers the opportunity to raise their future young in a safer forest habitat,” International Animal Rescue, YIARI’s founding partner, wrote in a statement.

It has been revealed that experts ultimately chose to release them at Batu Nyambu Protected Forest. While also in West Kalimantan, its roughly 23,000 hectares of land and nearby forests haven’t been affected by the recent fires. Batu Nyambu has plenty of natural food, fresh water, nesting trees, and space. But getting the females and their babies there wasn’t simple—they had to travel by road, boat, and on foot for a total of 12 hours. Luckily, they had support from local communities and traditional leaders.

“We are grateful for the support of the community, village governments and traditional leaders,” said Argitoe Ranting, YIARI’s Director of Operations. “The long-term success of conservation efforts depends not only on protecting the area, but also on the role of the people living around the forest in safeguarding habitat and preventing various threats to wildlife.”.

Most fires in Indonesia are associated with human activity such as using fire to clear land for plantations and agriculture.

The Intricate Textile Designs of William Morris Bring Into Conflict the Concepts of Art and Accessibility

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Born into a wealthy English family, William Morris (1834-1896) grew up in the countryside, honing a love for nature that found expression in fabric and wallpaper he designed for his successful firm, Morris & Tech giant.
  • But while he believed in a universal right to beauty, his own careful craftsmanship held a certain contradiction, says Amy George, curator of a retrospective of Morris’ original designs opening this month at the Whitworth Art Gallery in Manchester, England.
  • Perhaps ironically, in recent years capitalism has made Morris’ work more accessible, as it has appeared on products from mass-market brands like H&M and Williams Sonoma.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Born into a wealthy English family, William Morris (1834-1896) grew up in the countryside, honing a love for nature that found expression in fabric and wallpaper he designed for his successful firm, Morris & Tech giant. An activist as well as an artist and businessman, he loathed the inequity of Victorian society and the soullessness of the industrial age, coming to embrace revolutionary socialism.

But while he believed in a universal right to beauty, his own careful craftsmanship held a certain contradiction, says Amy George, curator of a retrospective of Morris’ original designs opening this month at the Whitworth Art Gallery in Manchester, England. “Anything handmade is expensive,” she notes. “And it should be expensive, because of the labor that goes into it.”.

Perhaps ironically, in recent years capitalism has made Morris’ work more accessible, as it has appeared on products from mass-market brands like H&M and Williams Sonoma. In a way, it seems, his goal of art for all may finally have been realized.

This article is a selection from the December 2026 concern of Smithsonian magazine.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that they may be small, but bear cubs have a pretty steep learning curve. In Alaska, brown bear (Ursus americanus) cubs have a roughly 50 percent survival rate within their first year, while the black bear (Ursus americanus) cub survival rate can range from 51 to 88 percent, depending on where they live. Cubs must learn how to fish, forage, find shelter, and climb trees to escape predators. Fortunately, biology helps out a bit with climbing. Bears have claws that curve and help them go up the tree and then back down safely.

One baby black bear who spent time at Anan Creek in southeastern Alaska’s Tongass National Forest revealed off those climbing chops in style. The park’s rangers have officially awarded this bear with the 2026 Cutest Climber Award.

“This little cub slipped on his way down but caught himself and hustled right after mom,” the rangers write. “An adorable reminder that even when you lose your footing, you can recover and keep going. A tiny, furry lesson in resilience provided by the bears of Anan.”.

Tongass National Forest’s rangers  are currently awarding the Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory in Alaska over the summer.

Tongass is the largest national forest in the United States, and covers most of southeastern Alaska, including the state’s capital city of Juneau. The area includes Mendanhall Glacier (a popular destination for tourists on Alaskan cruises), numerous hiking trails, eagles soaring above, and plenty of bears on the hunt for food. One of the hotspots is Anan Creek, home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in Southeast Alaska. As such, the creek is a very popular dinner spot among black and brown bears.

According to Friends of Anan, 39 bears are known to feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears and eight brown bears. Similar to  their chunky counterparts farther to the north in Katmai National Park, the bears return each summer to feast on salmon and teach their cubs how to fish in order to survive. And also like the fat bears of Katmai, every bear here has their own habits and quirks.

In a recent development, the U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear spotted at Anan, while explore.org’s cameras broadcast live streams of their antics.

Nuclear submarine returns from record-breaking 217 days underwater

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (579 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A nuclear submarine recently returned to Scotland after setting a Royal Navy record of 217 days underwater.
  • “The fleet was designed around three-month tours, and that was considered to be a long time to be stuck underwater in a metal box with no contact with the outside world,” nuclear submarine expert David Cullen told The Guardian on November 15.
  • The 17,526-ton, nearly 500-foot-long HMS Vengeance is one of Britain’s four Vanguard-class submarines constructed to carry monstrous Trident nuclear missiles.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A nuclear submarine recently returned to Scotland after setting a Royal Navy record of 217 days underwater. The HMS Vengeance’s seven-month deployment overtook the 205-day milestone set by the HMS Vanguard in April. But with the Vengeance crew finally back home, critics now argue the two submarines’ lengthy back-to-back voyages are causes for concern, not celebration.

“The fleet was designed around three-month tours, and that was considered to be a long time to be stuck underwater in a metal box with no contact with the outside world,” nuclear submarine expert David Cullen told The Guardian on November 15.

The 17,526-ton, nearly 500-foot-long HMS Vengeance is one of Britain’s four Vanguard-class submarines constructed to carry monstrous Trident nuclear missiles. First introduced in 1998, the vessel features 16 missile tubes, each loaded with one Trident containing up to a dozen, 100-kiloton multiple independently targetable reentry vehicles (MIRVs). The MIRV is specifically engineered to simultaneously deploy a payload of individual nuclear weapons aimed at a list of targets. The Royal Navy continuously keeps at least one Vanguard submarine at sea, which hypothetically allows the United Kingdom to still conduct nuclear strikes in the event its land-based systems are compromised during a nuclear war.

Vanguard submarines were originally built to host around 140 crewmembers during three-to-four month deployments. Although a 100-day excursion was once considered rare, underwater stints are now often double the length of time, forcing sailors to stack extra provisions along already cramped corridors and inside any additional nooks. The U.K. government attributes the extended missions to budgetary cuts that have dramatically slowed down the pace of multimillion-dollar vessel maintenance projects.

It has been revealed that deployment aboard a submarine like the Vengeance is considered one of the navy’s most psychologically difficult assignments. The nuclear sub remains underwater in total radio silence for the entire length of a patrol to keep its position secret. The vessel can travel to a depth of around 984 feet, but it may occasionally ascend to shallower waters to communicate via a transmission buoy or floating wire antenna. Crewmembers may receive a weekly, 120-word “Familygram” message, but each dispatch is previewed by naval officials. These readers retain the right to censor any bad news or information they feel may compromise sailors’ effectiveness. Regardless of what a sailor ultimately reads, they are strictly prohibited from responding.

The toll on crew is steep, but it’s particularly difficult for the women comprising roughly 10-percent of the navy. In 2022, whistleblower Sophie Brook generated international headlines after reporting a “constant campaign of sexual bullying” while serving as one of the Royal Navy’s first female submariners. In 2024, First Sea Lord Adm. Sir Ben Key called the crew misogyny “intolerable” and apologized to the growing number of women who subsequently came forward with their own stories. The Royal Navy’s investigations ultimately resulted in the firing, demotion, and disciplining of dozens of servicemen—including Key’s own termination.

Recent findings suggest that key’s successor, Gen. Sir Gwyn Jenkins, stated he had “nothing but tremendous respect” for Trident crews earlier this month, while admitting the need to “improve our submarine maintenance.”.

Industry observers note that the Vanguard fleet was designed for about 25 years of service, but will likely accumulate roughly four decades of sailing by the time its first replacement is ready. That submarine, the HMS Dreadnought, isn’t expected to sail until around 2032.

#330. Latest Update: Europe's Hera Spacecraft Has Begun Its Close-Up Investigation of the Asteroid System NASA Intentionally Hit in 2022

Latest Update: Europe's Hera Spacecraft Has Begun Its Close-Up Investigation of the Asteroid System NASA Intentionally Hit in 2022

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (916 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smithsonianmag

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The European Space Agency (ESA) has started its close-up investigation of an asteroid system smashed by NASA in 2022.
  • Industry observers note that ESA’s Hera spacecraft reached the Didymos binary asteroid system on November 4, more than two years after it launched from Cape Canaveral, Florida.
  • The asteroid Didymos is roughly 2,560 feet in diameter and has a companion moonlet called Dimorphos, which is about 495 feet in diameter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The European Space Agency (ESA) has started its close-up investigation of an asteroid system smashed by NASA in 2022.

Industry observers note that ESA’s Hera spacecraft reached the Didymos binary asteroid system on November 4, more than two years after it launched from Cape Canaveral, Florida. The mission will examine the aftermath of NASA’s Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) collision, helping scientists better understand how the technique could one day be used to protect Earth from incoming space rocks.

The asteroid Didymos is roughly 2,560 feet in diameter and has a companion moonlet called Dimorphos, which is about 495 feet in diameter. They form a binary asteroid system, a pair of asteroids that are gravitationally bound, orbiting each other around a shared center of mass.

Industry observers note that in September 2022, the golf-cart-size DART spacecraft intentionally struck the smaller celestial body in the world’s first demonstration of asteroid deflection technology. The mission not only successfully collided with Dimorphos, shortening its orbit around its major sibling by 33 minutes; it also altered the asteroid pair’s route around the sun. Now, Hera is returning to the crash scene to follow up on that work.

“Hera wants to be the detective, like Inspector Colombo, going back to the crash scene,” Patrick Michel, a planetary scientist at the French National Center for Scientific Research and Hera’s principal investigator, tells Meghan Bartels for Space.com.

The spacecraft, which is about the size of a small car, performed its first arrival maneuver on October 15, and ESA released Hera’s first close-up photo of the asteroid duo on November 5. The picture, snapped about 37 miles from the rocky pair, prominently features Didymos, with the smaller Dimorphos mostly hidden in the larger asteroid’s shadow.

In a recent development, while looking at this image, “the first thing we noted was wow!” Michel says in a statement. “This is the other side of Didymos from the one that DART’s camera showed us shortly before impact, so this feels like looking at a whole latest world.”.

Recent findings suggest that on November 12, ESA released another image of the asteroid system, this time taken from about 35 miles away. It highlights one side of Didymos and a sliver of Dimorphos peeking out from behind the larger rock, on the upper left. This photo reveals various features on the bigger asteroid’s surface, including large boulders, smooth areas and a sharp ridge at the equator.

Scientists want to understand which of these and other characteristics were present long ago and which might be consequences of the DART impact.

According to recent reports, “Since we expect a lot of impact-ejected material to have made it across the approximately one kilometer of space from Dimorphos to Didymos, it may be that some of these characteristics originate from this transport of material, and we have exciting work ahead of us to sort it out,” states Michael Küppers, a planetary scientist and Hera mission scientist at ESA, in the earlier statement. “We look forward to seeing much more of both bodies and systemically mapping all the changes we identify.”.

It has been revealed that hera should now be within about 20 miles of the asteroid duo, per Space.com, and then move even closer in December. Then, early next year, the spacecraft will deploy two shoebox-size CubeSats. These nanosatellites, equipped with radar and spectral instruments, will fly in and examine the surfaces and inner structures of the asteroids. One of the devices, called Juventas, will attempt to land on Dimorphos to capture more information about the asteroid’s surface material and gravity field.

According to recent reports, did you know? Complementary design.

The DART and Hera missions were intentionally designed to go together, with the first performing the deflection and the second collecting precise measurements of the outcome.

These studies will not just help experts develop techniques for planetary defense in case an object one day poses a danger to Earth; they’ll also advance our understanding of asteroids in general.

“Planetary defense and science are sort of two sides of the same coin,” notes Jessica Sunshine, a planetary scientist at the University of Maryland who was on the DART team but is not involved in the Hera mission, to Bartels for Science News. On the science side, she adds, “we’re trying to figure out not so much how did we break the thing, but how was it put together in the first place.”.

Industry observers note that one question she and other researchers hope Hera will help answer relates to the system’s stabilization post-impact. Previously, Dimorphos always indicated the same face to Didymos as it circled its companion, like the moon does with Earth. Researchers suspect DART changed that, and they want to see how it’ll reset, per Science News. Additionally, they want to better understand how exposure to charged particles affects an asteroid’s surface. The debris kicked up on Dimorphos by DART can help them examine fresh rock that was previously protected from those particles.

Detailed images of both asteroids will be unveiled on November 25, according to the earlier statement.

Recent findings suggest that “For us, it’s like a new world,” Michel tells Space.com. “The new image won’t have anything to do with the previous one, so that’s really exciting.”.

#326. More Than a Billion Years' Worth of Rock Layers Are Missing From Earth's Geologic Record. Scientists Say They May Finally Know Why

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (701 w)
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Smithsonianmag

More Than a Billion Years' Worth of Rock Layers Are Missing From Earth's Geologic Record. Scientists Say They May Finally Know Why

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (701 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smithsonianmag

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, rock layers record the Earth’s history, typically piling up from oldest at the bottom to youngest at the top.
  • Now, scientists say they may have figured out what caused the so-called Great Unconformity.
  • In a recent development, computer simulations hint the missing rock layers, which should be older than roughly 540 million years old, were uplifted by movements of Earth’s viscous mantle layer and eroded away by giant ice sheets before the continents sank back down again.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, rock layers record the Earth’s history, typically piling up from oldest at the bottom to youngest at the top. But a giant, mysterious gap exists in many of the globe’s landmasses. It’s well-documented in North America, northern Europe and northern China, where in some places more than one billion years of our planet’s geologic record is nowhere to be found.

Now, scientists say they may have figured out what caused the so-called Great Unconformity.

In a recent development, computer simulations hint the missing rock layers, which should be older than roughly 540 million years old, were uplifted by movements of Earth’s viscous mantle layer and eroded away by giant ice sheets before the continents sank back down again. The findings, published November 4 in the journal Nature, help validate some of the possible explanations about the Great Unconformity, possibly solving the 150-year-old mystery.

“Imagine a book where a huge section in the middle has been ripped out. The Great Unconformity is that gap in Earth’s story, with the narrative jumping from the early chapters straight to a much later part of the story,” says study co-author Santosh Dhungana, an Earth scientist at the University of Wollongong in Australia, in a statement. “Our research suggests these pages weren’t lost by chance.”.

Did you know? The Grand Canyon’s role.

Researchers first described the Great Unconformity in the late 1800s in the layers of the Grand Canyon.

It has been revealed that many scientists suspect that during the planet’s theorized Snowball Earth period, when the entire planet may have been frozen some 635 million to 720 million years ago, moving ice scraped away the missing rock layers. But if ice sheets covered the globe, they should have eroded the Great Unconformity everywhere, which isn’t the case, reports Ars Technica’s Jacek Krywko.

Sources indicate that some researchers have also hypothesized that mantle movements, which alter the planet’s surface, could be to blame. In the viscous mantle, hotter material rises and cooler material falls, pushing and pulling Earth’s outer layer, called the crust. However, this concept of mantle-driven dynamic topography “hadn’t been quantitatively tested,” study co-author Nicolas Flament, a geoscientist at the University of Wollongong, tells Ars Technica.

It has been revealed that so, he and Dhungana used computer models to simulate these mantle movements, called convection, over the past billion years. Their six models “consistently showed that mantle convection caused ancient continental blocks Laurentia (which now makes up much of North America), Baltica (parts of northern Europe) and North China to be lifted up from around a billion years ago to 540 million years ago,” the authors write for the Conversation. Over the past 540 million years, however, these continental chunks have sunk.

Industry observers note that the era of continental uplift overlaps with the Snowball Earth period, and giant moving ice sheets erode landscapes more efficiently than rivers. The scientists speculate that the frozen masses would have ground their way down the slopes of raised landscapes, wiping away millions of years’ worth of rock accumulation.

What’s more, the Great Unconformity intrigues scientists interested in life’s history because it wiped the rock record just before the Cambrian explosion around 530 million years ago, when all sorts of animals suddenly evolved.

In a recent development, the geologic processes that took place during the Great Unconformity may have created the foundation for this famous evolutionary event, Shanan Peters, a geoscientist at the University of Wisconsin-Madison who did not participate in the study, tells Live Science’s Stephanie Pappas. By exposing older crystalline rocks, for example, the erosion may have triggered a greater release of certain elements, such as potassium, iron, manganese and carbon, into the oceans, allowing marine life to invent shells. That, in turn, may have put more oxygen into Earth’s atmosphere, Peters adds.

“Sometimes what is missing can tell us more about the story of Earth than what we can see,” Flament claims in the statement.

#325. Solar recycling 2.0

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1715 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Pv-magazine

Solar recycling 2.0

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1715 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Pv-magazine

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A number of companies in the United States are vying to leverage capital, experience, and upcoming technology ahead of a wave of end-of-life solar panels expected in the coming years.
  • According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), the annual volume of end-of-life crystalline silicon modules in the US is expected to hit 87,000 metric tons (MT) by 2030 and skyrocket to 820,000 MT by 2050.
  • With that volume comes economic opportunity.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A number of companies in the United States are vying to leverage capital, experience, and upcoming technology ahead of a wave of end-of-life solar panels expected in the coming years.

According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), the annual volume of end-of-life crystalline silicon modules in the US is expected to hit 87,000 metric tons (MT) by 2030 and skyrocket to 820,000 MT by 2050.

With that volume comes economic opportunity. In 2023, analysts at Rystad Energy estimated the global value of recycled solar materials would hit $2.7 billion in 2030, rising to $80 billion by 2050. Assuming a 15-year panel lifespan, Rystad’s research estimated end-of-life solar modules in North America would be worth $1.4 billion in 2037 – about 15% of the global total.

This article appears in a special edition of pv magazine, produced for RE+ 2026 in Las Vegas. Scan or Click for free access to the full 54-page magazine, packed with the latest from the US solar and energy storage industries.

Sources indicate that most of the material in a solar module is glass, which typically accounts for between 70% and 76% of a module’s weight. The second-largest portion is the aluminum frame, accounting for between 8% and 13%. But the most valuable material inside most solar modules is silver.

Industry observers note that silver now represents an key strategic asset to the United States. Along with silicon, ­silver was added to the US Critical Minerals List in November 2025.

In solar manufacturing, paste formed with the precious metal is screen printed in thin lines onto the surface of a silicon solar cell to collect and transport electrical current. It accounts for around 60% of the cost of those cells, and 10% of the total cost of a solar module.

According to the IEA, solar silver consumption was around 10 mg/W in 2024, down from 16 mg/W in 2020. While this equates to only about 0.05% of a panel’s total weight, the concentration of silver in a solar module rivals that found in many silver ores currently being mined.

That number was even higher for modules produced further in the past, meaning the coming wave of end-of-life modules will be rich in their most valuable component. The trouble is, once the cells are sealed inside layers of encapsulant, the metal contents have proven very difficult to recover without a high-temperature smelting process.

It is common practice for PV recycling companies to separate the glass and frame on the outside of a module, while the laminated components on the inside are shredded and sent to other recyclers often overseas, or even to landfill.

“The industry as a whole up to now has been on a 1.0 system, if you will,” said Adam Saghei, CEO of We Recycle Solar (WRS), in an interview with pv magazine USA. “It’s about shredding. It is heavily dependent on a mechanical process.”.

When that shredded material is exported, the valuable silver, silicon, copper, and other trace metals trapped in the encapsulant are exported, too.

According to recent reports, in addition, the recovered glass often contains impurities that make it unsuitable for use in high-temperature, closed-loop remanufacturing, such as new solar glass, instead of being used in “down-cycled” applications such as road base, concrete aggregate, and sandblasting media. All of that is changing now.

A number of US companies have developed alternative technologies to capture a much greater proportion of valuable solar materials and sell them domestically.

In September, WRS declared that it planned to open what it called “the nation’s first end-to-end critical materials recovery facility for retired solar panels” on a 10-acre site in Dallas, Texas, by the third quarter of 2027. The company says its “recycling 2.0” process allows it to recover up to 96% of the silver, copper, silicon, aluminum, and glass from end-of-life solar panels.

Sources indicate that “Our approach is a little bit different,” said Saghei. “It’s on a very small footprint with regenerative solvents.” He added that the process results in glass with less than 10 parts per million of impurities. “That is essentially pure enough for you to drink out of. It’s as pure as glass comes.”.

In a recent development, meanwhile, OnePlanet Solar has been operating its commercial demonstration plant in Florida since early 2024. The plant is capable of processing 480,000 end-of-life solar modules in a year, equal to around 19,000 tons of material. According to the organization, 100% of the outputs of this facility have been sold and consumed within the United States.

In a recent development, in August 2026, OnePlanet unveiled its upcoming “PRISM” process (short for “Photovoltaic Recycling through Integrated Systems and Mechanics”). The firm notes PRISM results in 99% pure glass before any size reduction step, for both single side and bifacial modules, and also yields a concentrated silicon product with 95% purity that contains 1% silver.

Recycling of end-of-life modules using the PRISM process is expected to begin in 2027, and OnePlanet’s next goal is to refine its own metallurgical-grade silicon (MGS) while capturing the silver as a secondary finished product.

Industry observers note that another US firm building out its recycling capabilities is Comstock Metals, which is now in the beginning stages of operating a solar recycling facility in Silver Springs, Nevada. The facility was first commissioned and tested in August 2026, and the company is working to ramp the plant up to 25% of its rated output capacity of 100,000 tons per year.

Comstock is also practicing a upcoming, proprietary process at the Silver Spring site, designed to completely decompose adhesives, encapsulant, and plastic materials before the remaining components of the panel are sorted and separated for additional processing. Judd Merrill, the organization’s chief financial officer, explained that the company’s current strategy is to retain the metal-rich material for its own proprietary metals recovery process.

Comstock’s aims for that metal recovery process start with a pilot-scale metals recovery operation, also planned for Silver Springs. “We are developing proprietary extraction and recovery technologies specifically designed to process the concentrated material generated by our solar recycling system. That material contains multiple valuable metals and other recoverable materials, and our objective is to recover those materials into marketable products for domestic reuse without conventional smelting,” mentioned Merrill.

Comstock’s goal is to have a pilot-scale metal recovery line “operating continuously and reliably” by the end of 2026.

A key step in the success of any business is the development of ongoing relationships with partners. For solar recyclers, those relationships are made with entities on both sides of the recycling process.

On the supply side, this means contracting with manufacturers, EPCs, and re-powering companies. Comstock, for example, has minted deals with RWE for decommissioning aged solar panels as well as agreeing to take manufacturing byproducts from solar manufacturer Illuminate USA.

Sources indicate that similarly, leading recycler Solarcycle has partnered with Silfab, Canadian Solar, and Qcells to recycle factory defects and has inked agreements with major developers including Sunrun, EDP Renewables, AES, Orsted, and Greenbacker. The firm has also confirmed public offtake agreements for the outputs of its recycling process. It has signed agreements with Silfab and Illuminate USA for new solar glass made from recycled modules.

Solarcycle is at the moment in the process of building a 1.1 million square foot glass plant next to its existing recycling facility in Cedartown, Georgia. With glass production at the facility slated to begin in 2028, the company is targeting enough glass production to support up to 6 GW of domestic panel assembly annually.

As of 2025, the NC Clean Energy Technology Center tracked 23 states with mandatory statewide decommissioning policies. Despite the widespread nature of those policies, laws in just four states (California, Maine, New Jersey, and New York) effectively prohibit the disposal of solar panels in landfills and dumps.

Outside those states, and in the absence of federal regulation, entities seeking to responsibly offload those products usually engage recyclers based on their own corporate ESG goals.

It has been revealed that obtaining quality and traceability certifications has become a key way recyclers set themselves apart from their competitors. Recyclers often pursue certification under ISO standards 9001 (Quality Management Systems), 14001 (Environmental Management Systems), and 45001 (Occupational Health and Safety).

In addition to obtaining those certifications, many companies seek listing under the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA) National PV Recycling Program, which requires a facility audit and analysis of a tech giant’s operations. SEIA at the moment lists 16 companies as partners under the program.

According to recent reports, recyclers seeking to go one step further obtain a certification from Sustainable Electronics Recycling International (SERI), which certifies PV recyclers under Appendix G of the third version of its Responsible Recycling (R2v3) standard. R2v3 requires annual surveillance audits by accredited certification bodies and complete chain of custody documentation for all materials. It also enforces safe handling procedures for panels, solar glass processing standards, and silicon wafer recovery protocols.

At the time of writing, SERI lists 30 facilities with active R2v3 certifications in North America, including the Comstock and OnePlanet facilities.

“Our view of certifications is pretty straightforward,” Connor Hogan, CFO of OnePlanet, told pv magazine USA. “If you can get a certification, you should just get a certification rather than say that you can attest to it.”.

Industry observers note that other companies aren’t as keen on R2v3. “One glitch with R2 certification is that it’s kind of open source, and when you spend years cultivating a relationship with a downstream partner, you don’t want to just give that up so everyone knows who you’re selling material to,” remarked Saghei, adding that “certifications are like a driver’s license – just because everyone has one doesn’t mean they’re a good driver.”.

In the coming years, solar recyclers will find many ways to differentiate themselves based on the effectiveness and economics of their logistics and recovery processes, as well as the adaptability of those processes and how swiftly they can scale operations.

It has been revealed that the relationships recyclers build with manufacturers, developers, downstream offtakers, and policymakers will also be essential. They will face questions from those stakeholders about their certifications and material tracing practices and will likely be presented with fresh challenges as state governments take action to ensure solar module waste is recycled properly.

#324. Peeping woodcocks are evolutionary oddballs

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (518 w)

Peeping woodcocks are evolutionary oddballs

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (518 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As far as birds go, the eight known species of woodcock (genus Scolopax) look like they specifically evolved to go viral on the internet.
  • Woodcocks are part of the larger sandpiper family, but unlike their migratory relatives, most only travel extremely short seasonal distances.
  • Industry observers note that “The distribution of woodcocks and snipes around the world is really unusual,” John Bates, the curator of birds at the Field Museum’s Negaunee Integrative Research Center in Chicago, remarked in a statement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As far as birds go, the eight known species of woodcock (genus Scolopax) look like they specifically evolved to go viral on the internet. You’ve probably seen at least a few videos of the birds on social media darting across beaches and being incredibly vocal. As if their small, squat bodies and comically long beaks weren’t enough, they also vocalize with distinctively cartoonish peeping tweets during their mating displays.

Woodcocks are part of the larger sandpiper family, but unlike their migratory relatives, most only travel extremely short seasonal distances. Six of the eight species are only found on specific islands, and some of them don’t even migrate at all. So how did these evolutionary oddballs even get their start—and stop migrating? To piece together their unique avian story, biologists analyzed the DNA of all eight woodcock species and 22 species of snipe.

Industry observers note that “The distribution of woodcocks and snipes around the world is really unusual,” John Bates, the curator of birds at the Field Museum’s Negaunee Integrative Research Center in Chicago, remarked in a statement. “They’re not terribly aerodynamic, and yet they’ve clearly gotten around.”.

Recent findings suggest that bates and his colleagues published the results of their work today in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS). The years-long endeavor involved not only examining preserved woodcock specimens housed in the Field Museum, but a fossilized sandpiper previously excavated from a cave site in Haiti. The remains found on the island of Hispaniola are around 1,000 years old, but that is still extremely young in the grand history of shorebirds.

The earliest members of the sandpiper family began in the northern hemisphere before slowly migrating to islands along lower latitudes. Those birds subsequently migrated much shorter distances after settling in the warmer climates. However, they didn’t remain sedentary. Based on the DNA analysis detailed in their study, Bates and his team theorize that snipes from Africa eventually traveled across the Atlantic Ocean, then evolved into fresh species in South America. From there, more of the birds made their way over the Pacific Ocean to New Zealand.

According to recent reports, their examinations also cleared up a bit of confusion. Biologists initially believed the fossilized sandpiper from Haiti was a woodcock, but the most recent data now shows that it’s a snipe.

Recent findings suggest that “Snipes and woodcocks have been around for 20 to 25 million years,” Bates explained. “Over that time, as newly introduced species have evolved and moved around the world, their migratory patterns have changed, too.”.

These changes are likely to continue amid today’s dramatic climate shifts, but that may pose a problem for the beloved woodcocks.

According to recent reports, “These are definitely birds that would be affected by changing habitats and changing climates,” remarked Bates. “Some of these woodcocks are found only in the mountain forests on islands between Asia and Australia, and if those forests get cut down, the birds are going to be gone too.”.

#322. Latest Update: A French Court Annuls the $1.6-Million Sale of This Camille Pissarro Painting, Allegedly Looted During World War II

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (941 w)
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Smithsonianmag

Latest Update: A French Court Annuls the $1.6-Million Sale of This Camille Pissarro Painting, Allegedly Looted During World War II

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (941 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smithsonianmag

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, in 1941, German forces in occupied Paris looted a Jewish banker’s collection of impressionist artworks.
  • A 1902 landscape by Camille Pissarro titled Darse de pêche et bassin Duquesne, Dieppe, après-midi ensoleillée (Fishing Dock and Duquesne Basin, Dieppe, Sunny Afternoon) was auctioned by Sotheby’s London on June 25, 2024, to an anonymous buyer for roughly $1.6 million.
  • Between 1933 and 1945, the Nazi regime orchestrated the largest art theft in history, seizing more than 650,000 artworks across Europe—some 20 percent of the continent’s art—including from Jewish families, collectors and museums.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, in 1941, German forces in occupied Paris looted a Jewish banker’s collection of impressionist artworks. Now, more than eight decades later, a French court has stepped in to demand the return of one allegedly looted painting to the descendants of its owner.

A 1902 landscape by Camille Pissarro titled Darse de pêche et bassin Duquesne, Dieppe, après-midi ensoleillée (Fishing Dock and Duquesne Basin, Dieppe, Sunny Afternoon) was auctioned by Sotheby’s London on June 25, 2024, to an anonymous buyer for roughly $1.6 million. On November 5, the Paris Judicial Court annulled that sale and ordered Sotheby’s to “disclose the full identity of the buyer of the work” within two months or pay a $1,115 fine for every additional day it fails to do so, CNN’s Lianne Kolirin reports.

Between 1933 and 1945, the Nazi regime orchestrated the largest art theft in history, seizing more than 650,000 artworks across Europe—some 20 percent of the continent’s art—including from Jewish families, collectors and museums.

Salomon Flavian, a Jewish banker of French and Romanian heritage, purchased Pissarro’s view of the Normandy port town of Dieppe at the Hôtel Drouot auction house in Paris in March 1935, according to the Sotheby’s listing.

When war erupted in September 1939, Flavian placed the canvas and dozens of other works into the care of the Westminster Foreign Bank in Paris. In 1941, German forces seized his collection. Although Flavian survived the war and recovered some pieces, the Pissarro remained missing and was listed in France’s official register of looted property.

Nearly eight decades later, the painting resurfaced at Sotheby’s London with a note stating that it was “offered for sale pursuant to a settlement between the current owner and heirs of Salomon Flavian.” That settlement had been brokered by the Mondex Corporation, a Toronto-based firm specializing in recovering Nazi-looted art.

Industry observers note that at a hearing in this fall, seven descendants of Flavian told the court that two relatives had signed the deal without consulting the rest of the family. The descendants claimed they had only found out about the sale months later, when Mondex sent a letter explaining that it had accepted in their name a “relatively modest” 8 percent share of the net sale price “in exchange for their cooperation,” while the two heirs who signed the contract received a 16 percent commission, the Art Newspaper’s Vincent Noce reported in September.

Recent findings suggest that at the hearing, Sotheby’s and Mondex presented research claiming that Flavian had parted with the painting before the war, pointing to a 1939 Pissarro catalogue raisonné by Paris dealer Paul Rosenberg that listed British artist and collector Edward Le Bas as the owner. Sotheby’s auction provenance similarly traced the canvas from Flavian to Rosenberg by 1937 and to Le Bas by 1939. It then eventually passed through several American collections, including David Rockefeller’s, and a 1985 sale at Sotheby’s Upcoming York.

According to recent reports, earlier this month, the Paris court rejected that timeline, finding “no direct and convincing evidence” of prewar sales to Rosenberg or Le Bas, according to the Art Newspaper. Instead, the court concluded that the family presented “a set of precise, serious and concurring elements demonstrating that Pissarro’s work was indeed looted during” the war.

The court ordered “the restitution of the work, wherever and in whoever’s possession it may be, to the descendants of Salomon Flavian,” the London Times’ David Chazan reports.

“It is a very important ruling, which opens the way to a restitution that the Flavian family has demanded since the war,” Corinne Hershkovitch, the claimants’ lawyer, tells the Art Newspaper.

Did you know? Looted art on display.

In May, the Musée d’Orsay in Paris opened a new permanent exhibition titled “Who Owns These Works?” It showcases 13 artworks that may have been looted or sold under suspicious circumstances during World War II with the hope that public exposure may help locate the rightful owners.

Mondex, which was ordered to pay $11,000 to the heirs, plans to challenge the verdict. Mondex founder James Palmer tells ARTnews’ Brian Boucher that an appeal will be filed “forthwith.” He adds: “We are confident that when the vast amount of complex provenance research evidence is properly understood and considered that the court of appeal will reach a different conclusion.”.

Because the French judgment applies immediately despite any appeal, the legal battle now shifts toward enforcing the order across the English Channel. Hershkovitch, however, tells the Times that cross-border enforcement between France and England is “a fairly simple procedure.” She adds: “Sotheby’s will have to find a solution very rapidly because their reputation is at stake.”.

Recent findings suggest that in a statement, Sotheby’s London noted its disappointment in the verdict, welcomed the dismissal of charges against the auction house and recognized the “profound losses suffered by the Flavian family during the Nazi era,” per CNN. A spokesperson indicates that Sotheby’s is considering whether to join Mondex’s appeal, while stressing that “client confidentiality is of paramount importance,” according to the Art Newspaper.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that over the past 17 months, the Wildlife Conservation Society’s Bronx Zoo in New York City has rescued dozens of parrots from the illegal pet trade. They include white-fronted Amazons (Amazona albifrons) and orange-fronted conures (Eupsittula canicularis).

The United States Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) confiscated the orange-fronted conures during three separate operations over the last 17 months, and the white-fronted Amazons in the last several months. All of the birds were discovered at the U.S.–Mexico border.

It has been revealed that “These animals were stolen from the wild and are victims of the illegal wildlife pet trade, and our responsibility is to give them the best possible chance for a healthy future,” Chuck Cerbini, WCS Bronx Zoo Curator of Ornithology, noted in a statement. “Working with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, our veterinary and animal care teams provide specialized expertise to assess, treat, and care for confiscated wildlife.”.

When confiscated wildlife arrives at the Bronx Zoo, the veterinary and animal care teams first conduct a health check, provide any necessary medical treatment, and then help find long-term placements for those that can’t be released into the wild.

White-fronted Amazons are native to parts of Mexico and Central America and represent the smallest Amazon parrot. They are also one of the few parrot species in which males and females feature visibly different plumage. Both sexes have a white foreheads, red faces, and yellowish bills, but males have red shoulders and females have green shoulders.

Orange-fronted conures, also known as half-moon conure or Petz’s conure, are also native to parts of Mexico and Central America, where they live in open woodlands, forest edges, and savannas. They have an orange forehead and green and blue feathers.

Sources indicate that the IUCN Red List categorizes both birds as a species of Least Concern, but that still  doesn’t justify trafficking them in the illegal pet trade. Parrots throughout Latin America are subject to both the loss of forest habitat and poaching.

Birds in particular l are especially threatened by trafficking because they are valued in the pet trade and the collector trade.

Industry observers note that one of the rarest and most coveted coins in United States history is headed for the auction block this week, where it could sell for over $2 million. But while collectors have long dreamed about owning one of the five existing 1885 silver trade dollars, the strange story of their creation remains murky more than 140 years after their minting.

The U.S. struck the first trade dollars in 1873 as a way to compete with similar silver coinage in East Asia, but the production was short-lived. Silver market fluctuations and foreign policy shifts led to their demonetization in 1876, and they were only minted for collectors beginning in 1879. By 1884, the U.S. commissioned only 10 trade dollars before finally retiring the series destroying the die casts.

Recent findings suggest that however, a thoroughly corrupt political appointee named A. Loudon Snowden had other looks. Snowden’s career in currencies began in 1857, when his uncle and former Treasurer of Pennsylvania hired the then 22-year-old whippersnapper at the Philadelphia Mint. While at the mint, he pursued various personal profiteering interests, including the clandestine production and selling of thousands of rare coins for collectors.In 1885, Snowden finally retired as Superintendent of the Philadelphia Mint after nearly three decades.

Snowden also gave himself a parting gift before retiring—five 1885 trade dollars that he purchased from the Mint cashier. No one knew of their existence until a year after Snowden’s death in 1912. The first 1885 trade dollar auctioned in 1913 for $1,140 (about $32,174 in current valuation).

Although some numismatists and historians argue Snowden’s five trade dollars were a final grift, other experts argue that the coins have a surprisingly mundane backstory. Until the 1930’s, Mint employees were legally allowed to purchase examples of latest coinage for their equivalent amount. Snowden did just this when he previously bought 10 proof 1884 trade dollars, and it’s possible he bought the following year’s coins before the decision not to mint any others. Regardless of the true story, only five 1885 trade dollars exist today—and they’re worth far more than Snowden could ever imagine.

Stack’s Bowers will auction the 1885 trade dollar as part of its Rarities Night series on Tuesday, November 17.

A 16th-Century Castle in England Is Falling Into the Ocean, Sparking a Debate Over Whether It Should Be Saved or Allowed to Disintegrate With Dignity

  • Sources indicate that as the beach gradually eroded away, the castle’s foundations first started to poke through the rocks in 2017, growing weaker each year.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For centuries, Hurst Castle, built on England’s south coast by Henry VIII in 1544 to protect the passage to Portsmouth, was unassailable. Through Tudor spats with France and the Holy Roman Empire, the English Civil War, skirmishes with Napoleon and both world wars, the squat artillery fort was garrisoned and at the ready, but never once attacked. After sitting almost at sea level for four centuries unchallenged, the castle is now under attack from a different sort of enemy, one even more pernicious than the French. Climate change, in the form of rising tides and worsening storms, is washing out the rocky beach from underneath Hurst’s walls.

Sources indicate that as the beach gradually eroded away, the castle’s foundations first started to poke through the rocks in 2017, growing weaker each year. Then, in 2021, its east-facing wall collapsed.

It has been revealed that standing on the eroded shore in front of Hurst on an overcast morning in 2024, castle keeper Jason Crane recalled the calm February day of the breach. He pointed to a gash of rubble where the east wing used to face the waves. “The whole of that wall ejected,” he said. “It puked right out into the sea” and left a 38-ton cannon rolling down onto the beach. Crane has known Hurst since he was a child, playing with crab shells through its halls while his grandfather was castle keeper, so the destruction was wrenching to watch. “The noise was something really low and horrible,” he remembered. “I definitely took it to heart.” Crane means that literally: a month after the collapse he suffered a heart attack from stress.

It has been revealed that in all likelihood, that 2021 collapse was just the opening salvo in a slow siege which could eventually destroy entire sections of the castle. That would mean the end of one of Britain’s most fascinating historical mosaics: 20th-century concrete bunkers built on a Victorian extension of a Tudor venture in castle making.

If you go: Other Tudor castles worth visiting.

Crane, working in concert with English Heritage, the charity that runs England’s historic monuments, has worked on several aims to save the site before the waves come crashing through. After coastal modeling and 3D surveys of the castle’s foundations, engineers estimate they can buy Hurst another few decades. But the work would cost more than £6 million (around $7.5 million), and time is already short. After the first collapse, engineers wired dozens of sensors through the precarious east wing to watch for signs of the next break. “You can’t just leave a pile of rocks,” noted Crane. “It’s definitely going to be a painful process.”.

Hurst therefore presents a fork in the road for English Heritage: fight to preserve a jewel in the country’s historical crown or start curating its transition from a castle into a ruin.

Sources indicate that rob Woodside, who joined Crane in the quest to solve this problem, showed me around the site in October 2024. For the seven years he spent as a director at English Heritage, Woodside worried about Hurst. “It’s a race against time,” he said.

It has been revealed that hurst sits on a small headland. The spit connecting it to the mainland is not as reliable as it used to be, so like most visitors we took a small boat, the Henrietta Rose, steered by a beanie-wearing pilot. As the castle’s outline came into focus, Woodside got nervously animated. “It always feels a little bit like a school trip … really exciting,” he remarked. “And then on the way back I’m more depressed,” he shrugged, “because, oh God, all that we’ve got to do.”.

Industry observers note that from the roof of the Tudor keep—now ringed with World War II anti-aircraft swivels—Woodside’s voice was almost drowned out by an ominously churning patch of water at the foot of the castle walls. Once inside the castle, Woodside walked me up a flight of stairs: “This is the global classroom,” he mentioned, opening the door to Hurst’s old barracks. On the large, wood-paneled floor, we encountered a big, dark puddle. “A leak,” he muttered, craning his neck at the ceiling. “Oh God, please not more.”.

Industry observers note that subsequent monarchs after Henry VIII added to Hurst to protect it against new advances in warfare, not from waves. Each of the Victorian wings is built from heavy Norwegian granite to protect canons and their crews from enemy fire. In the 20th century, the Ministry of Defense added anti-aircraft turrets—all on top of a brick foundation built directly on the beach. Since its first Tudor incarnation, Hurst has become more than a little top-heavy.

As the foundations wore away, in fact, the entire west wing started to rotate under its own weight, spinning slowly and gloomily out toward the sand. From the central keep, I saw a snaking crack along the roof where the structure was beginning to tear away into the water.

Woodside had wanted to be more proactive than previous government stewards of the castle. In 2019, a couple of years into his tenure, English Heritage spent more than $900,000 replenishing the sand and installing wooden barricades to stabilize the castle. But the beach kept disappearing, and those barricades appear to have backfired, casting up particularly aggressive torrents of water during storms. Two years later, of course, the wall collapsed anyway. It became clear, Woodside remarked, that the only way to protect Hurst in the long-term was to try to hold back the sea itself.

First, engineers suggested dropping huge boulders underwater to break up tidal surges. The catch: boulders significant enough to do the job (20 tons each) would have to be shipped from Norway. This strategy, which Woodside called the “gold-plated” approach, would likely have protected the castle for around a century, at a cost of more than $137 million. That would’ve been a landscape-changing feat of engineering that Woodside simply stated was “not for us.”.

Blueprint B still involves substantial boulders—but slightly smaller and strategically placed at the surf line. These rocks would disrupt the flow of water approaching the castle, creating a calmer area where sand doesn’t wash away so swiftly. They would protect the castle for only a few decades, engineers estimate, before the rocks would need maintenance themselves. But an imperfect plan is better than no plan, stated Woodside, and crucially, the smaller rocks cost only the equivalent of roughly $7.5 million.

In a recent development, through most of our interviews, Woodside remained cautiously optimistic about raising that sum. Saving the castle for decades would cost about as much as running the British health service for 15 minutes—his point being that the work might be expensive by heritage standards, but only a drop in the bucket of overall public finances.

In a recent development, then, a month after I visited, the British government’s body for protecting heritage sites rejected Woodside’s pitch. “We had a bit of a crunch, really,” he said when we caught up later. Not long after the news, he left English Heritage.

The decision didn’t just mark the end of Woodside’s hopes of saving Hurst, but the beginning of a strange, liminal time for the castle. Britain has historically notable buildings, and it has historical sites where buildings used to be. As the destruction slowly continues, Hurst is sliding into some uncomfortable middle ground between the two.

According to recent reports, engineers predict that water will finally enter the castle via the first wall that collapsed. “Eventually you’ll have to start to close the western end, then the property entirely, on safety grounds,” Woodside noted. Woodside left emergency instructions behind for when the water starts to break through: which artifacts to remove first; how to shut down the site’s generator. “Basically, you’re in a process of ruination. You’re going from a structure to an archaeological monument.”.

Industry observers note that that means taking stock of the castle “block by block,” said Matt Thompson, a curator at English Heritage who has taken responsibility for Hurst since Woodside left. Archaeologists and curators will give the castle a complete “family history,” after which Thompson wants to bring in locals to build an oral history of the site. “If you think you might lose something, capturing its memory is really key,” he said. “It’s like a grieving process.” Meanwhile engineers will monitor the sensors to gauge when health and safety concerns start to override this memorialization; parts of the castle will gradually grow unsafe and be cordoned off.

According to recent reports, after the first collapse and his heart attack, Crane entered counseling to deal with the stress and, he said, guilty  feelings. Now he is finished with grieving. “I probably took too much to heart,” he said. “You have to detach; I step back from it a lot more emotionally now.” He is even prepared to be merciless about how to save the castle, suggesting tearing down the newer Victorian wing before it falls in a storm and damages the Tudor parts in the process. “The same gun emplacements are replicated a number of times through the castle,” he said. “How do you choose which part of history is vital?”.

Recent findings suggest that thompson was keen to stress that English Heritage has not committed to a single plan nor to letting Hurst simply “fall into the sea.” Still, he offers a different view on the changes shaking the castle. “You can’t stand there and turn the tides,” he said. “[But] there are lots of things you can do to try and preserve the idea of a place, even if its actual fabric is under severe pressures.”.

In a recent development, hurst will not be the first ruins wrought by climate change. From old slave-trading forts in Ghana to Ernest Shackleton’s Antarctic expedition hut on Ross Island, conservationists are working to save waterfront monuments from warming and rising oceans. Droughts brought the Cambodian city of Angkor to its knees in the 15th century, while in modern-day Scotland, some historians think sea level rise, not Vikings, may have displaced Pictish settlements in the sixth century. Nor will Hurst be the last climate ruin: In August, academics from the United Kingdom, Greece and South Africa published a list of nearly 400 coastal World Heritage Sites that are at risk from erosion, storms and rising seas.

Perhaps Hurst will still be a flagship for coastal monuments, just not in the way English Heritage first thought: not a model of preservation, but the herald of a newer, more sweeping era of curated ruination. “We can choose to see that as something we want to arrest … or we can begin to embrace the beauty that comes with the different stages of the life of a place, a thing, a person,” Thompson said. “Impermanence is actually quite a beautiful thing.”.

Eagles will typically defend their nest from intruders so Shadow’s willingness to share his space with an eagle other than Kaydee surprised many viewers.

Shadow returned the nest solo later in the afternoon as the sun set over Significant Bear Lake.

Dark Energy Survey/DOE/FNAL/ DECam/CTIO/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA.

Sources indicate that joshua Frieman remembers when the world found out that the universe was made of much more than just matter. For a few years, the scientist had been studying the possibility that the cosmos needed something else — a “missing energy” — to make sense. But it was a niche idea. When he and a colleague started to blueprint a workshop on the topic in 1997, at first only a few dozen people signed up. Then, in early 1998, two teams of researchers revealed that exploding stars called supernovas seemed to be racing away from Earth under the influence of an unidentified, omnipresent repellent force. The observations implied the existence of exactly the sort of missing energy that Frieman and his colleagues planned to talk about.

“Suddenly, everyone wanted to come to our workshop,” including reporters with TV cameras, remarked Frieman, now at the University of Chicago. It was “kind of a circus.”.

In a recent development, within a few years, cosmologists had arrived at a whole new view of reality. The missing energy, given the name “dark energy” for its invisible nature, was pushing galaxies apart. The energy seemed embedded in space itself. It made up roughly two-thirds of creation (with matter — visible and dark — making up the remainder). Frieman embarked on what would become a two-decade mission to learn about dark energy by watching how it influences all that we can see: the Dark Energy Survey (DES).

In a recent development, now that project has come to a close. In May 2026, DES shared findings based on its full dataset of thousands of supernovas and hundreds of millions of galaxies spanning billions of years of cosmic history. Those findings, in combination with data gathered by a different project, the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI), suggest that our understanding of what the universe is made of — the venerable “standard model” of cosmology — is not complete. “There appear to be cracks in that model,” remarked Simone Ferraro, a cosmologist at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. “There’s something that doesn’t fit.”.

Joshua Frieman, a physicist at the University of Chicago, co-founded the Dark Energy Survey to examine the accelerating expansion of the universe.

Cosmologists can’t yet say what that something is. What they can say is that after 20 years of stability, their field is returning to a state of confusion. “It’s certainly enough to make you either uncomfortable or excited,” Ferraro stated.

In a recent development, experimental cosmology is a piecemeal endeavor. It’s a bit like trying to reconstruct a person’s life from a dossier of data about them: report cards, utility bills, cholesterol tests, and so on. You come up with a story that weaves all the data together, go find new data, and use it to refine the story. Frieman and other cosmologists started to speculate about a missing form of energy in the mid-1990s because the story they were telling didn’t seem quite right.

It has been revealed that in previous decades, they had peered at the sky and inferred roughly how much stuff was out there. They saw a smattering of galaxies lighting up the void — visible matter. Based on how fast the galaxies were spinning, astronomers deduced that a preponderance of invisible matter must surround each bright speck, holding it together — dark matter.

The rate at which these galaxies were receding from view implied that the universe had been expanding for some 8 billion to 13 billion years. It looked as if there was just enough matter (dark and visible combined) to tug gravitationally on the universe and continuously slow this expansion without ever bringing it to a full halt.

Industry observers note that but newly introduced observations started to clash with this accounting. Astronomers spotted stars, for instance, that seemed to be older than the universe. While trying to understand these and other anomalies, cosmologists noticed that it helped to add a new type of energy to their models.

It has been revealed that then came the bombshell 1998 findings that the expansion of the universe was not actually slowing down; it was ever so slightly speeding up. By the end of the year, the unknown stuff driving that acceleration had a name: dark energy. Frieman charged off to measure it.

In 1998, cosmologists were like detectives with a thin dossier. They had a blurry image of light from the early universe known as the cosmic microwave background (CMB). And they had observed several million galaxies, along with dozens of supernovas. Because light takes time to travel, these observations gave cosmologists snapshots of what the universe looked like at different moments over the past few billion years.

The Dark Energy Camera holds an array of charge-coupled devices, or CCDs, similar to the sensors in normal digital cameras but designed specifically for astronomy.

It has been revealed that DOE/FNAL/DECam/R. Hahn/CTIO/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA.

In a recent development, that was just enough data to show that the universe was experiencing an unexpected growth spurt. But to figure out exactly when it had started and how fast it was happening, Frieman and his colleagues would need to fatten their file. Their solution was DES.

In a recent development, DES began in 2003, with a handful of physicists at Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory brainstorming what it would take to get a more comprehensive view of the cosmos. They went on to design and build the 570-megapixel Dark Energy Camera, the most powerful digital camera of its era, and install it on the 4-meter-wide Blanco telescope in the Chilean Andes. They then used it to conduct the Dark Energy Survey, which ran for 758 nights between 2013 and 2019. During this time, DES increased the number of recorded galaxies to hundreds of millions. DES was supposed to end in 2018, but the researchers extended it to make up for lousy observations due to clouds from a strong El Niño season.

According to recent reports, every couple of years the DES collaboration, which grew to include more than 400 scientists across seven countries, would analyze the data they had collected so far to see what it suggested about the history of our universe. Again and again, what they found was consistent with the theory that had coalesced after the 1998 supernova papers: The universe was about 30% matter (mostly an invisible and lethargically drifting “cold dark matter,” or CDM), and the remaining 70% of the universe was dark energy. Physicists noted that this energy acted like an unchanging property of the vacuum of space, referred to as “lambda.” The bigger space gets, the more of this vacuum energy there is, and the faster the cosmos expands. This theory of the universe became known as Lambda-CDM.

In a recent development, then, in 2024, researchers from a next-generation experiment, DESI, combined the DES observations with a sharper image of the CMB and new observations of their own. They found that the Lambda-CDM theory no longer quite fit.

Whereas DES uses one big camera in Chile, DESI at Kitt Peak in Arizona uses thousands of tiny eyes. Each can swivel to focus on a single galaxy. The individualized attention more precisely captures each galaxy’s motion.

According to recent reports, this technology lets DESI see hidden cosmic structures. Due to the way that sound waves rippled through matter in the early universe, spherical shells of slightly dense matter formed. Over time, matter in these shells gathered into galaxies. Each shell is the same size, so by looking at how substantial or small it appears from Earth, scientists can tell how far away its galaxies are.

Combining the distances to the galaxies with other observations, the researchers can calculate how fast the universe has grown over the past 10 billion years or so (out of the 13.8 billion years since the Major Bang).

Young stars emitting stellar winds shaped the dust and gas of the Dragon nebula, captured here by the Dark Energy Camera, into a form that resembles a pair of fighting dragons.

Dark Energy Survey/DOE/FNAL/ DECam/CTIO/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA.

In 2024, the DESI collaboration dropped a bombshell report. When researchers added their shells to the existing dossier, they couldn’t get the Lambda-CDM model to fit all the data. What fit better was an exotic theory that replaced lambda, the constant vacuum energy, with a different form of energy that weakened over time. A year later, an analysis of more data found the same thing.

It has been revealed that in the meantime, the DES collaboration continued to analyze the galaxies they had photographed. Those researchers focused on building a different contribution to the dossier: a detailed record of a cosmic tug-of-war.

It has been revealed that while gravity pulls matter — mostly dark matter — together, dark energy fights back, pushing matter apart. By measuring how much matter has clumped together in different eras, cosmologists can infer the strength of dark energy over time.

DES assesses this clumping using three methods, explained Sujeong Lee, a physicist at Ohio University. First, DES measures how tightly galaxies of visible matter cluster together, which reveals how much dark matter floats around them. Second, it maps out visible matter in the foreground by looking for the ways it distorts light coming from galaxies in the background. And third, it maps out foreground dark matter in a similar way.

Industry observers note that each of these measurements involves comparing pair after pair of DES’s hundreds of millions of galaxies, looking for tiny distortions in their positions and shapes. After seven years of rigorous analysis, the collaboration published their final results in early 2026. “It’s been a real tour de force,” remarked Ferraro, who isn’t part of DES. “It pushed the analysis to a newly introduced level.”.

In a recent development, alongside these measurements, DES also reprocessed a catalog they had compiled of 1,600 recently observed supernovas, establishing the sharpest view yet of the modern universe. “I trust the DES-reanalyzed supernova data much more than I trust any other supernova dataset,” said Seshadri Nadathur, a DESI cosmologist.

Recent findings suggest that cosmologists have now assembled their thickest file on the universe to date. DES merged its map of matter clumping, its supernova catalog, DESI’s galaxy shells, and a CMB image, then checked to see how well Lambda-CDM could still account for the whole cosmic history.

The answer: not very well. In their final report, DES scientists found that their data fit somewhat better with the theory that dark energy is not stable and has slackened in recent eons. In the statistical language of physicists, DES reports a “three-sigma” preference for the new theory. That’s significant enough to make people pay attention, especially since it combines data collected in different ways, but it falls far short of the “five-sigma” confidence physicists need to claim a new discovery.

Industry observers note that the Dark Energy Camera was mounted on the Victor M. Blanco 4-Meter Telescope, famous for its role in the 1998 discovery that the expansion of the universe is accelerating, a process thought to be driven by dark energy.

CTIO/NOIRLab/DOE/NSF/AURA/R. Hahn (Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory).

Adding to the intrigue, DES found that the mismatch can’t be explained away if, for instance, one of the datasets holds some hidden error. If you assume Lambda-CDM is right, the CMB picture doesn’t quite match the matter maps; the matter maps don’t quite match the supernovas; and the supernovas don’t quite match the CMB picture. There is no single item that you can toss from the file to make everything fit, so no single observation looks fishier than the others.

This suggests that the tension is less likely to be a random artifact — the kind that could easily arise from the merger of millions of observations using different instruments — and is more likely to reflect a clash between the real universe and our understanding of it. “There’s something that doesn’t fit,” Ferraro stated. And “we’re trying to figure out what that something is.”.

Sources indicate that some theorists are deeply skeptical of the idea that dark energy can change. They already face a major challenge in explaining why the vacuum of space has the specific energy that it seems to have — an almost imperceptible amount of oomph filling every cubic kilometer of space. Confirmation that dark energy is also changing would layer on a second major challenge: explaining why that mysteriously tiny amount of energy is evaporating at a mysteriously slow rate.

Some cosmologists wonder if they should tweak other assumptions of Lambda-CDM instead, such as the time at which early stars (and possibly other bright objects) burnt off a hydrogen fog that filled the early universe. Lambda-CDM puts this event at roughly 700 million years after the Significant Bang. But if this happened roughly 200 million years earlier, Ferraro and collaborators found in a 2025 analysis, then Lambda-CDM would fit the cosmological data better. “This number is crucial,” Ferraro said. “However, it’s extremely hard to measure.”.

Sources indicate that the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, seen here, sits on Cerro Pachón, about six miles from Cerro Tololo, the home of the Dark Energy Survey.

RubinObs/NOIRLab/SLAC/NSF/DOE/AURA/A. Pizarro D.

Other theorists are looking into the implications of a changing dark energy, such as the possibility that it could shift in tandem with the mass of dark matter.

For observational cosmologists, the next steps are clear: Keep fattening the dossier on the universe. While DES has ended, DESI will continue collecting data until at least 2028. And on the summit of Cerro Pachón in Chile, the Vera C. Rubin Observatory started its survey operations in 2026.

Rubin is a spiritual successor to DES. It now holds the honor of hosting the world’s largest digital camera, and astronomers expect its powerful eye to spot roughly 10 billion — with a “b” — galaxies. DES veterans are already flocking to the Rubin collaboration to help analyze those galaxies, pair by pair, just as they did for DES.

Recent findings suggest that back in the 1990s, the quickening expansion of the universe became clear from the motions of just a few dozen supernovas. Rubin should find millions more. In a dossier comprised of millions of supernovas and billions of galaxies, an exquisitely detailed cosmic history — and an accounting of the forces that shaped it — will be laid bare for all to see.

#315. Latest Update: These Adorable Hatchlings Are From the U.S. West Coast's First Known Natural Sea Turtle Nests. Now, They've Returned to the Wild

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Smithsonianmag

Latest Update: These Adorable Hatchlings Are From the U.S. West Coast's First Known Natural Sea Turtle Nests. Now, They've Returned to the Wild
